Phenylalanine accumulates and converts into phenylpyruvic acid and other derivatives (II), leading to mental retardation and reduced pigmentation (IV).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 90: 'This inborn error of metabolism is inherited as the autosomal recessive trait. The affected individual lacks an enzyme that converts the amino acid phenylalanine into tyrosine. As a result of this, phenylalanine is accumulated and converted into phenylpyruvic acid...'

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of events during the inheritance of ABO blood groups showcasing multiple allelomorphism and co-dominance?
options: Presence of gene I with three alleles (I^A, I^B, i) -> Production of respective sugar polymers on RBC surface -> Expression of co-dominance when both I^A and I^B are present together
Production of co-dominant sugars -> Mutation of allele i -> Expression of multiple alleles
Expression of phenotype 'O' -> Production of enzymes by allele i -> Co-dominance of alleles I^A and i
Formation of hybrid sugars by allele i -> Dominance of I^A over I^B -> Absence of antigen on RBC
questions.explanation: The gene I controls ABO blood grouping and has three alleles (I^A, I^B, i). The alleles I^A and I^B produce slightly different forms of the sugar polymer on the RBC surface, while allele i produces no sugar. When both I^A and I^B are present together, both express their own types of sugars, exhibiting co-dominance.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 77: 'The plasma membrane of the red blood cells has sugar polymers that protrude from its surface and the kind of sugar is controlled by the gene I... The alleles I^A and I^B produce a slightly different form of the sugar while allele 'i' does not produce any sugar... When I^A and I^B are present together they both express their own types of sugars: this is because of co-dominance.'

questions.question:
Arrange the following genetic events chronologically according to Mendel's hybridization experiments in pea plants:
I. Selection of 14 true-breeding pea plant varieties
II. Crossing of contrasting pure lines to produce F1 generation
III. Self-pollination of F1 generation to produce F2 generation
IV. Formulation of laws of inheritance based on statistical analysis of F2
questions.explanation: Mendel first selected 14 true-breeding pea plant varieties (I). He then crossed contrasting pure lines to obtain the F1 generation (II), self-pollinated F1 to obtain the F2 generation (III), and finally formulated his laws of inheritance based on the mathematical and statistical analysis of F2 data (IV).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 70-74: Mendel selected 14 true-breeding pea plant varieties, performed artificial hybridization/cross-pollination to create F1, selfed F1 to get F2, and proposed principles/laws.

questions.question:
Sequence the steps involved in identifying sex in grasshopper (XO type mechanism):
I. Male produces two types of gametes (50% with X, 50% without X)
II. Female produces eggs all bearing X chromosomes (XX)
III. Fertilization determines whether offspring receives one X or two X chromosomes
IV. Offspring with XO develop into males and XX into females
questions.explanation: In grasshoppers, females have two X chromosomes (XX, producing ova all with X - II), while males have only one X chromosome (XO, producing 50% sperms with X and 50% without X - I). Fertilization determines the zygotic chromosomal constitution (III), leading to XO males and XX females (IV).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 85: 'In a large number of insects the mechanism of sex determination is of XO type... females, have a pair of X-chromosomes (XX) and male(s) have only one X-chromosome besides the autosomes... sperms bear the sex-chromosome (X) as well as some without it.'

questions.question:
Arrange in correct order the cellular events that occur during the formation of a Barr body (Lyonisation) in normal human females:
I. Random inactivation of one of the two X chromosomes during embryonic development
II. Condensation of the inactivated X chromosome into a heterochromatin mass
III. Dosage compensation so that functional X-linked gene product is equivalent in both sexes
IV. Presence of condensed chromatin visible as Barr body at the nuclear periphery
questions.explanation: During early embryonic development in human females, one of the two X chromosomes is randomly inactivated (I), condenses into a heterochromatic mass (II), becomes visible as a Barr body at the nuclear periphery (IV), achieving dosage compensation with males (III).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 86-87: Discusses sex determination and dosage compensation implicitly linked to X-chromosome behavior (Note: Barr body concept is part of standard NCERT-aligned chromosomal basis of sex determination).

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of events when a carrier female of hemophilia marries a normal male?
options: Parental genotypes set as X^hX and XY -> Segregation during gametogenesis yielding X^h, X and X, Y gametes -> Combination producing 25% normal daughters, 25% carrier daughters, 25% normal sons, 25% hemophilic sons
Parental genotypes set as XX and X^hY -> Offspring all hemophilic -> Lethal in utero
Parental genotypes set as X^hX^h and XY -> All sons hemophilic and all daughters carriers
Parental genotypes set as XX and XY -> Segregation yielding no diseased offspring
questions.explanation: A carrier female has genotype X^hX and a normal male has XY. During gametogenesis, the female produces X^h and X gametes, while the male produces X and Y gametes. Fertilization results in 25% normal daughters (XX), 25% carrier daughters (X^hX), 25% normal sons (XY), and 25% hemophilic sons (X^hY).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 89: 'The possible result of such a marriage [carrier female and normal male] can be understood... haemophilic son (25%), carrier daughter (25%)...'

questions.question: In a typical pedigree chart analysis, what does a filled square symbol conventionally represent?
questions.explanation: In standard pedigree analysis used in human genetics (as per NCERT), squares represent males, circles represent females, and shading or filling of the symbol indicates the affected individual expressing the trait.
questions.ncertEvidence: Pedigree analysis chart symbols: Square for male, circle for female, and filled symbols for affected individuals.

questions.question: Identify the chromosomal representation of an individual affected with Down's syndrome, which arises due to the presence of an additional chromosome number 21.
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is trisomy of chromosome 21. Since total chromosomes are 47 (45 + XY for males or 45 + XX for females), option 2 correctly represents the chromosomal constitution (45 autosomes + sex chromosomes XY).
questions.ncertEvidence: Down's syndrome is characterized by trisomy of chromosome 21, leading to a total of 47 chromosomes (45 + XY or 45 + XX).

questions.question: Based on the standard representation of pedigree charts, which of the following symbols indicates mating between relatives (consanguineous mating)?
options: A single horizontal line connecting a square and a circle
Two horizontal lines connecting a square and a circle
A vertical line dropping from a mating line to offspring
questions.explanation: In pedigree charts, consanguineous mating (mating between close relatives) is specifically represented by a double horizontal line connecting the male and female symbols.
questions.ncertEvidence: Standard pedigree symbols: Mating between relatives is represented by two horizontal lines.

questions.question: Which of the following diagrams or crosses best illustrates the phenomenon of incomplete dominance where the phenotypic ratio deviates from Mendel's monohybrid cross?
options: Cross between homozygous tall and dwarf pea plants resulting in tall F1
Cross between red-flowered (RR) and white-flowered (rr) Mirabilis jalapa resulting in pink-flowered (Rr) F1
Cross between yellow round and green wrinkled seeds resulting in four phenotypes
Cross between normal and sickle-cell hemoglobin expressing codominance
questions.explanation: Incomplete dominance is classically demonstrated in snapdragon (Antirrhinum majus) or four o'clock plant (Mirabilis jalapa) where a cross between red (RR) and white (rr) produces pink (Rr) flowers in the F1 generation.
questions.ncertEvidence: Incomplete dominance in dog flower (snapdragon or Antirrhinum sp.) where Rr is pink.

questions.question: In a dihybrid cross depicted on a Punnett square for seed shape and seed color in pea plants, how many genotypes are theoretically produced?
questions.explanation: A dihybrid cross involves two gene loci, each with 3 possible genotypes ($3 \times 3 = 9$). The Punnett square has 16 boxes (representing combinations of gametes), but the total number of unique genotypes is 9.
questions.ncertEvidence: Dihybrid cross phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1 and genotypic ratio comprises 9 different genotypes.

questions.question: When studying Drosophila melanogaster linkage and recombination, Morgan observed that genes located very close on the same chromosome showed:
questions.explanation: Morgan found that physical association of genes on a chromosome is linkage. Genes close together show very low recombination (tight linkage), whereas genes far apart show higher recombination.
questions.ncertEvidence: T.H. Morgan's linkage and recombination experiments on Drosophila showing tighter linkage for genes close together.

questions.question: Which chromosomal abnormality is correctly matched with its respective phenotypic syndrome described in NCERT?
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21). Klinefelter's is 44+XXY, Turner's is 44+XO, and Phenylketonuria is an autosomal recessive single-gene disorder.
questions.ncertEvidence: Chromosomal disorders: Down's syndrome (trisomy 21), Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY), Turner's syndrome (XO).

questions.question: In the representation of test cross progeny to determine the genotype of a tall pea plant, if all offspring are tall, the unknown parent genotype is:
questions.explanation: In a test cross, an organism with an dominant phenotype is crossed with the homozygous recessive parent (tt). If all progeny are dominant (tall), the test organism must be homozygous dominant (TT).
questions.ncertEvidence: Test cross definition and interpretation: crossing with recessive parent to determine zygosity.

questions.question: What is the primary reason why Thomas Hunt Morgan selected Drosophila melanogaster for his genetic experiments instead of pea plants?
options: They have a very long life cycle of about 2 years
They cannot be grown easily in synthetic medium in the laboratory
They complete their life cycle in about two weeks and produce a large number of progeny
They possess only one pair of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Morgan chose Drosophila because they could be grown easily in simple synthetic medium, complete their life cycle in about two weeks, and a single mating produces a large number of progeny.
questions.ncertEvidence: Suitability of Drosophila for genetic studies: 2-week life cycle, huge progeny, clear sexual dimorphism.

questions.question: Which of the following genetic disorders is an example of an X-linked recessive trait that shows a criss-cross inheritance pattern?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia is a classic X-linked recessive disease. It shows characteristic criss-cross inheritance where a carrier female passes the trait to her sons.
questions.ncertEvidence: Hemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disease with transmission from carrier mother to son.

questions.question: Based on a typical dihybrid cross in Drosophila conducted by T.H. Morgan, if two genes show very tight linkage, what percentage of parental types is typically observed in the F2 generation?
questions.explanation: Morgan found that genes linked very closely on the same chromosome showed very low recombination (e.g., 1.3% recombination in yellow-white cross), meaning the parental types constitute the overwhelming majority, approximately 98.7%.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 83, Figure 5.11 (Linkage and Recombination).

questions.question: In a pedigree chart analysis, what does a filled square symbol universally represent?
questions.explanation: Standard pedigree symbols dictate that squares represent males and circles represent females. A filled (darkened) symbol indicates an affected individual, hence a filled square represents an affected male.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 89, Figure 5.13 (Pedigree Analysis symbols).

questions.question: Examine the schematic representation of a pedigree showing inheritance of a trait. If unaffected parents produce an affected offspring, what mode of inheritance is immediately indicated?
questions.explanation: When unaffected parents give birth to an affected child, the trait must be recessive because both parents are heterozygous carriers without showing symptoms themselves.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 89-90, Pedigree analysis explanation.

questions.question: In a test cross involving F1 dihybrid flies where genes are physically associated on the same chromosome, the physical representation of recombinant types in progeny arises due to:
questions.explanation: When genes are linked on the same chromosome, recombinant progeny are formed solely due to crossing over (exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes) during meiosis.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 83, Linkage and Recombination section.

questions.question: Refer to the Punnett square representation of a monohybrid cross for flower color in Pisum sativum. If 'R' is completely dominant over 'r', what is the genotypic ratio depicted among the F2 offspring?
questions.explanation: The monohybrid cross genotypic ratio is distinctly 1 homozygous dominant (RR) : 2 heterozygous (Rr) : 1 homozygous recessive (rr), whereas the phenotypic ratio is 3:1.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 73, Mendel's Law of Segregation.

questions.question: In the graphical representation of chromosomal theory of inheritance, Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri pointed out that the pairing and separation of a pair of chromosomes would lead to the segregation of a pair of factors they carried. This behavior closely parallels:
options: Behavior of alleles during gamete formation
Replication of DNA strands during S-phase
questions.explanation: Sutton and Boveri noted that the behavior of chromosomes is parallel to the behavior of genes (factors) noted by Mendel, both occurring in pairs and segregating during gamete formation.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 81, Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance.

questions.question: Which of the following schematic representations correctly depicts the sex-determination mechanism seen in grasshoppers?
questions.explanation: In grasshoppers, sex determination is of the XO type, where males have only one X chromosome besides autosomes, and females have a pair of X chromosomes.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 86, Sex Determination section.

questions.question: When observing a karyotype diagram of an individual affected by Down's syndrome, what specific chromosomal abnormality is visualized?
options: Deletion of short arm of chromosome 5
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21, resulting in trisomy 21, which is clearly visible as three chromosomes at position 21 in a karyotype.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 91, Genetic Disorders.

questions.question: In a pedigree diagram representing a family with hemophilia, an affected male transmits the mutant allele to:
options: None of his sons, but all of his daughters as carriers
All of his sons and none of his daughters
Half of his sons and half of his daughters
questions.explanation: Hemophilia is an X-linked recessive trait. An affected male passes his single X chromosome only to his daughters (making them carriers) and his Y chromosome to his sons.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 90, Pedigree Analysis and Sex-linked inheritance.

questions.question: What is the primary visual feature in a pedigree chart that distinguishes an autosomal dominant trait from an autosomal recessive trait?
options: Autosomal dominant traits do not skip generations, whereas recessive traits can skip generations.
Autosomal dominant traits only affect females, whereas recessive traits affect males.
Autosomal dominant traits always show a 3:1 ratio in every single family.
Autosomal dominant traits require both parents to be affected.
questions.explanation: A key hallmark of dominant inheritance in pedigrees is that it appears in every generation without skipping, whereas recessive traits frequently skip generations through unaffected carriers.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 89-90, Pedigree Analysis.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms was extensively used by T.H. Morgan and his colleagues to study principles of heredity and variation, leading to the discovery of linkage?
questions.explanation: T.H. Morgan selected Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly) as the experimental organism because they could be grown on simple synthetic medium in the laboratory, have a short life cycle, and produce a large number of progeny per mating.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 80: 'Morgan worked with the tiny fruit flies, Drosophila melanogaster...'

questions.question: In the classical experiments on incomplete dominance, which plant was utilized by Carl Correns to demonstrate that the phenotypic ratio deviates from Mendel's monohybrid ratio?
questions.explanation: Mirabilis jalapa (4-o'clock plant) or Snapdragon (Antirrhinum majus) are classic examples used to demonstrate incomplete dominance, where the cross between red and white flowers yields pink flowers in the F1 generation.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 75: 'In a cross between true-breeding red-flowered (RR) and true-breeding white-flowered (rr) plants in dog flower (snapdragon or Antirrhinum sp.), the F1 was pink...'

questions.question: Human blood group inheritance controlled by the I gene is a classic textbook example of which genetic phenomenon involving multiple allele interactions?
questions.explanation: The ABO blood groups in humans are controlled by gene I which has three alleles (IA, IB, and i). When both IA and IB are present together, they both express their own types of sugars, showing co-dominance.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 77: 'The gene (I) controls the ABO blood grouping... alleles IA and IB produce a slightly different form of the sugar while allele i does not produce any sugar. ... When IA and IB are present together they both express their own types of sugars: this is because of co-dominance.'

questions.question: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inborn error of metabolism in humans that exhibits which of the following genetic modes of inheritance and effect?
options: Autosomal dominant trait exhibiting polygenic control
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the gene encoding phenylalanine hydroxylase. It exhibits pleiotropy as a single gene mutation results in multiple phenotypic expressions such as mental retardation and reduced hair/skin pigmentation.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 90: 'Phenylketonuria... The affected individual lacks an enzyme that converts the amino acid phenylalanine into tyrosine... resulting in mental retardation, reduction in hair and skin pigmentation.'

questions.question: Which of the following chromosomal disorder examples in humans is characterized by a karyotype with 47 chromosomes due to the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21?
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is caused by the presence of an additional copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy of chromosome 21), resulting in a total chromosome count of 47.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 92: 'Down's syndrome... This is caused by the presence of an additional copy of chromosome number 21 (trisomy of 21).'

questions.question: In honeybees, sex determination is based on the number of sets of chromosomes an organism receives. What term best describes the genetic makeup and origin of males in this system?
questions.explanation: In the haplo-diploid sex determination system of honeybees, the males (drones) are haploid and develop from unfertilized eggs by parthenogenesis, whereas females (workers and queens) are diploid.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 88: 'The sex determination in honey bees is based on the number of sets of chromosomes an individual receives. An offspring formed from the union of a sperm and an egg develops as a female (queen or worker), and an unfertilized egg develops as a male (drone) by means of parthenogenesis.'

questions.question: Which of the following human traits studied by Mendel in pea plants or analogous pedigree analysis represents an autosomal dominant condition?
questions.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy is an example of an autosomal dominant disorder in humans. Sickle-cell anaemia, phenylketonuria, and haemophilia are recessive disorders (haemophilia being X-linked recessive).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 89: 'Myotonic dystrophy... is an autosomal dominant trait.'

questions.question: Klinefelter's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder in humans arising from non-disjunction during gametogenesis. What is the typical sex-chromosome complement associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter's syndrome is caused by the presence of an additional X chromosome resulting in a karyotype of 47, XXY.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 92: 'Klinefelter's Syndrome... This disorder is also caused due to the presence of an additional copy of X-chromosome resulting into a karyotype of 47, XXY.'

questions.question: Which organism was used by Henking in 1891 to trace a specific nuclear structure through spermatogenesis, which he designated as the 'X body'?
questions.explanation: Henking (1891) traced a specific nuclear structure during spermatogenesis in insects (specifically the bug Pyrrhocoris) and called it the X body, which was later identified as the X chromosome.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 86: 'Henking (1891) could trace a specific nuclear structure all through spermatogenesis in a few insects, and it was also observed by him that 50 percent of the sperm received this structure after spermatogenesis, whereas the other 50 percent did not receive it. Henking gave a name to this structure as the X body...'

questions.question: Turner's syndrome is characterized by the absence of one of the X chromosomes in human females. What is the precise chromosomal formula for individuals affected by this condition?
questions.explanation: Turner's syndrome is caused by the absence of one of the X chromosomes, resulting in a karyotype of 45 with 44 + XO.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 92: 'Turner's syndrome... Such disorders is caused due to absence of one of the X chromosomes, i.e., 45 with XO.'

questions.question: Where are the genes for Mendelian characters located in eukaryotic cells, which act as the units of inheritance?
questions.explanation: Mendel's factors (now called genes) are located on chromosomes, which segregate and assort independently during meiosis, governing the inheritance of traits.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 69: 'Chromosomes as well as genes occur in pairs. The two alleles of a gene pair are located on homologous sites on homologous chromosomes.'

questions.question: During which meiotic stage do the two alleles of a gene pair separate from each other, ensuring that each gamete receives only one allele?
questions.explanation: The segregation of alleles (Law of Segregation) takes place during anaphase I when homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 72: 'The behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis can be used to explain Mendel's laws... the two alleles of a gene pair segregate during gamete formation.'

questions.question: What is the primary function of tRNA during polypeptide synthesis in the context of transmitting genetic information from DNA?
options: To read the genetic code on mRNA and bring specific amino acids to the ribosome
To form the structural backbone of the ribosome
To replicate genetic material in the nucleus
questions.explanation: While this question touches upon molecular biology often integrated with inheritance, tRNA acts as an adapter molecule that reads mRNA codons and translates them into amino acid sequences.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5 and 6 context on flow of genetic information; tRNA functions as an adapter molecule.

questions.question: In humans, which chromosome determines the sex of the individual, functioning as the chromosomal basis of male heterogamety?
questions.explanation: In human males, the presence of the Y chromosome determines the male sex, making them XY (heterogametic), whereas females are XX (homogametic).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 83: 'In a large number of insects and mammals including humans, sex determination is of XO type or XY type... males produce two different types of gametes (XY type).'

questions.question: What is the function of the centromere during cell division phases such as mitosis and meiosis?
options: It serves as the attachment site for spindle fibres (kinetochores) to pull sister chromatids apart
It synthesizes ribosomal RNA during interphase
It replicates DNA independently of the rest of the chromosome
It codes for regulatory enzymes of the cell cycle
questions.explanation: The centromere holds sister chromatids together and provides the site (via kinetochores) where spindle fibers attach during cell division.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5 context on chromosome morphology and behavior during segregation.

questions.question: Where do mutations, defined as sudden heritable changes in DNA sequence, ultimately exert their functional phenotypic effects?
options: By altering the amino acid sequence of proteins or modifying gene expression
By changing the nuclear membrane structure directly
By permanently halting all cellular respiration
By instantly doubling the entire somatic chromosome number
questions.explanation: Mutations alter the nucleotide sequence of DNA, which can lead to changes in mRNA codons, resulting in altered protein structure or function (as seen in point mutations like sickle-cell anaemia).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 87: 'Mutations is a phenomenon which results in alteration of DNA sequences and consequently results in changes in the genotype and the phenotype of an organism.'

questions.question: What is the specific cytological function of the enzyme recombinase during pachytene of meiotic prophase I?
options: It catalyses the exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
It completely dissolves the nuclear membrane before prophase
It aligns chromosomes at the equatorial plate during metaphase
It unzips the DNA double helix during DNA replication
questions.explanation: Recombinase mediates crossing over—the exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during pachytene stage.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 78: 'Crossing over is also an enzyme-mediated process and the enzyme involved is called recombinase.'

questions.question: In Drosophila melanogaster, what was the primary reason Morgan used linked genes to establish the concept of linkage and recombination?
options: Genes located on the same chromosome were found to be inherited together more frequently than expected by independent assortment
Linked genes always segregated into separate cells without exception
Linked genes underwent higher frequencies of crossing over than non-linked genes
The physical distance between linked genes was always zero
questions.explanation: Linkage describes the physical association of genes on a chromosome; genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together (parental combinations) unless separated by recombination.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 77: 'Morgan coined the term linkage to describe this physical association of genes on a chromosome and the term recombination to describe the generation of non-parental gene combinations.'

questions.question: What is the function of pedigree analysis in human genetics?
options: To trace the inheritance of a specific trait through generations of a family to study its pattern of inheritance
To artificially alter human chromosomes for therapeutic purposes
To count the exact number of base pairs in the human genome
To determine the rate of mitosis in embryonic tissues
questions.explanation: Pedigree analysis is the study of family histories to track the inheritance of traits or disorders across generations, helping determine if a trait is dominant, recessive, autosomal, or sex-linked.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 85: 'The analysis of traits in a several of generations of a family is called the pedigree analysis. The inheritance of a particular trait is represented in the family tree over generations.'

questions.question: What is the cellular consequence of non-disjunction of chromosome 21 during gametogenesis?
options: It leads to the production of gametes with an abnormal number of chromosomes, resulting in conditions like Down's syndrome upon fertilization
It causes the complete destruction of all cellular organelles
It triggers immediate programmed cell death in all somatic tissues
It increases the rate of transcription of all autosomal genes
questions.explanation: Failure of chromosomes to segregate properly during cell division (non-disjunction) results in aneuploidy, such as trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 90: 'The failure of segregation of chromatids during cell division cycle results in the gain or loss of a chromosome(s), called aneuploidy... Down's syndrome is due to trisomy of chromosome 21.'

questions.question: Which specific structural component of tRNA is responsible for reading the genetic code by pairing with the complementary sequence on mRNA?
questions.explanation: The anticodon loop has bases complementary to the code, which is the codon on the mRNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, page 110

questions.question: In the structural organization of human DNA, what is the primary function of the negatively charged phosphate backbone?
options: To allow intercalation of mutagenic dyes
To bind basic proteins like histones and provide structural stability
To form catalytic sites for transcription
To directly read the sequence of amino acids
questions.explanation: DNA is negatively charged due to the phosphate backbone, which allows it to wrap around positively charged basic amino acid residues of histones to form nucleosomes.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, page 99

questions.question: How does the structural presence of a 2'-OH group in the ribose sugar of RNA influence its functional stability compared to DNA?
options: It makes RNA more stable and less reactive
It makes RNA catalytic and more easily degradable (reactive)
It prevents the formation of phosphodiester bonds
It allows permanent storage of genetic information in all organisms
questions.explanation: The 2'-OH group present at every nucleotide in RNA is a reactive group that makes RNA labile and easily degradable, unlike DNA which lacks this group.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, page 109

questions.question: What is the structural consequence of purines pairing exclusively with pyrimidines across the double helix in DNA?
options: It creates a variable width along the DNA strand
It results in a uniform distance between the two strands of the helix
It forces the formation of single-stranded loops
questions.explanation: A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine across the double helix, which generates a uniform distance between the two strands of the helix.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, page 97

questions.question: Which structural feature of eukaryotic mRNA is added post-transcriptionally at the 5' end to facilitate translation and protect it from exonucleases?
questions.explanation: In capping, an unusual nucleotide (methyl guanosine triphosphate) is added to the 5'-end of hnRNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, page 113

questions.question: During DNA replication, why is the synthesis discontinuous on one of the template strands (the lagging strand)?
options: DNA polymerase can only polymerize in the 3' to 5' direction
DNA polymerase must synthesize in the 5' to 3' direction while the template opens in the 3' to 5' direction
RNA primers cannot attach to the leading strand
Ligase joins nucleotides in the opposite direction
questions.explanation: Because replication proceeds in the 5' to 3' direction, continuous synthesis occurs on the template with 3' to 5' polarity, while discontinuous synthesis occurs on the 5' to 3' template, producing Okazaki fragments.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, page 106

questions.question: What is the structural role of lactose acting as an inducer in the lac operon model?
options: It binds to the operator region to block RNA polymerase
It binds to the repressor protein, inactivating it and preventing it from binding to the operator
It directly transcribes the structural genes z, y, and a
It degrades the promoter region to initiate transcription
questions.explanation: The inducer (lactose/allolactose) binds to the repressor protein, causing it to be inactivated so it cannot bind to the operator region, allowing transcription to proceed.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, page 117

questions.question: Which structural characteristic distinguishes euchromatin from heterochromatin in terms of transcriptional activity?
options: Euchromatin is densely packed and transcriptionally inactive
Euchromatin is loosely packed and transcriptionally active
Heterochromatin is loosely packed and stains lightly
questions.explanation: The chromatin that is more loosely packed and stains light is called euchromatin, which is transcriptionally active, whereas heterochromatin is densely packed and inactive.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, page 101

questions.question: What is the specific function of the enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase in protein synthesis?
options: To form peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids
To charge tRNA by covalently linking it to its specific amino acid
To cleave introns from primary transcripts
To unwind the DNA double helix during transcription
questions.explanation: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase is responsible for charging the tRNA (loading it with its specific amino acid) using ATP.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, page 114

questions.question: In a nucleosome core particle, how many base pairs of DNA are wrapped around the histone octamer?
questions.explanation: A typical nucleosome contains 200 bp of DNA helix wrapped around a histone octamer, with the core particle specifically wrapping around 146 bp.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, page 99

questions.question:
Arrange the correct sequential steps involved in the process of a standard Dihybrid Cross as performed by Mendel, starting from the parental generation to the production of F2 phenotypes:
1. Selection of pure-breeding parents with contrasting traits for seed shape and seed color
2. Production of F1 generation showing dominant phenotype
3. Self-pollination of F1 plants to produce the F2 generation
4. Observation of phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation (9:3:3:1)
questions.explanation: Mendel's dihybrid cross starts with selecting pure-breeding parents (round yellow and wrinkled green), crossing them to get F1 heterozygotes, selfing F1 to produce F2, and finally observing the 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio.
questions.ncertEvidence: Principles of Inheritance and Variation, Section on Dihybrid Cross, detailing the crossing of pure lines, F1 generation, selfing, and F2 phenotypic ratio.

questions.question:
What is the correct sequence of events during the chromosomal theory of inheritance linking meiosis to segregation of Mendelian factors (genes)?
1. Pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I
2. Separation of homologous chromosomes at anaphase I
3. Separation of sister chromatids at anaphase II
4. Formation of haploid gametes carrying single allele for a trait
questions.explanation: During meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair up in prophase I, separate during anaphase I (which causes segregation of alleles), followed by sister chromatid separation in anaphase II, ultimately resulting in haploid gametes.
questions.ncertEvidence: Principles of Inheritance and Variation, Section on Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance, explaining how meiosis parallels the behavior of chromosomes and genes.

questions.question:
Identify the correct chronological or procedural order of steps when Mendel conducted hybridization experiments:
1. Selection of true-breeding parental lines
2. Emasculation (removal of anthers from the female parent before dehiscence)
3. Pollination using pollen from the male parent
4. Bagging of the emasculated flower to prevent contamination
questions.explanation: The procedural steps of artificial hybridization in plant breeding experiments involve selecting true-breeding parents, emasculation of the bisexual flower, bagging to prevent unwanted pollination, and dusting pollen onto the stigma.
questions.ncertEvidence: Principles of Inheritance and Variation, Section on Mendel's Laws of Inheritance, detailing methods of hybridization like emasculation and bagging.

questions.question:
In the mechanism of sex determination in human beings, arrange the following steps in correct sequence from gametogenesis to zygote formation resulting in a female child:
1. Meiosis in male resulting in X-bearing and Y-bearing sperms
2. Meiosis in female resulting in exclusively X-bearing eggs
3. Fusion of an X-bearing sperm with an X-bearing egg
4. Development of zygote into a female individual (XX)
questions.explanation: Both males and females undergo meiosis simultaneously to produce gametes (sperms with X or Y, and eggs with X only). Fusion of an X sperm and X egg forms an XX zygote, which develops into a female.
questions.ncertEvidence: Principles of Inheritance and Variation, Section on Sex Determination, explaining male and female heterogamety and fertilization outcomes.

questions.question:
What is the correct sequence of molecular and cellular events leading to sickle-cell anemia manifestation?
1. Substitution of Glutamic acid (Glu) by Valine (Val) at the 6th position of the beta-globin chain
2. Point mutation in the beta-globin gene (GAG to GUG)
3. Polymerization of mutant hemoglobin under low oxygen tension
4. Alteration of RBC shape from biconcave disc to elongated sickle shape
questions.explanation: The sequence starts with a point mutation in the DNA (GAG to GUG), leading to amino acid substitution (Glu to Val), which causes mutant hemoglobin molecules to polymerize under low oxygen, changing the RBC shape into a sickle.
questions.ncertEvidence: Principles of Inheritance and Variation, Section on Sickle-cell anemia, detailing the molecular basis and structural change in hemoglobin and RBCs.

questions.question:
Arrange the following stages in the diagnostic cytogenetic analysis of Down's syndrome from a patient:
1. Collection of a tissue sample (like blood) and culturing cells
2. Arresting cell division at metaphase using colchicine
3. Staining and preparation of karyotype to examine chromosome 21
4. Identification of trisomy (three chromosomes at position 21)
questions.explanation: Cytogenetic analysis involves culturing cells, arresting them at metaphase, staining for karyotyping, and finally identifying chromosomal abnormalities like trisomy 21.
questions.ncertEvidence: Principles of Inheritance and Variation, Section on Chromosomal Disorders (Down's Syndrome), describing trisomy resulting from non-disjunction.

questions.question:
Trace the correct sequence of events during gamete formation in an individual heterozygous for two linked genes (e.g., 'AB' in cis/coupling configuration) when crossing over occurs:
1. Pairing of homologous chromosomes in pachytene
2. Crossing over and exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids
3. Separation of chromosomes during anaphase I and chromatids in anaphase II
4. Formation of both parental (AB, ab) and recombinant (Ab, aB) gametes
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes pair up during prophase I (pachytene), crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids, followed by meiotic divisions to produce both parental and recombinant gametes.
questions.ncertEvidence: Principles of Inheritance and Variation, Section on Linkage and Recombination, detailing the mechanism of crossing over during meiosis.

questions.question:
What is the correct sequence of steps in pedigree analysis when studying the inheritance pattern of a specific genetic trait in a family?
1. Collection of phenotypic data of family members over multiple generations
2. Construction of family tree using standard symbols
3. Analyzing the pedigree to determine if the trait is dominant, recessive, autosomal, or sex-linked
4. Predicting the risk of transmission of the trait to future offspring
questions.explanation: Pedigree analysis begins with gathering phenotypic data, drawing the pedigree tree, analyzing inheritance patterns based on standard rules, and finally predicting risks for offspring.
questions.ncertEvidence: Principles of Inheritance and Variation, Section on Pedigree Analysis, outlining the utility and interpretation of family trees for genetic traits.

questions.question:
Arrange the following events in the correct chronological order of discovery and formulation in classical genetics:
1. Mendel's publication of inheritance laws in experiments on plant hybridization
2. Rediscovery of Mendel's results by de Vries, Correns, and von Tschermak
3. Sutton and Boveri proposing the chromosomal theory of inheritance
4. Thomas Hunt Morgan proving linkage and recombination using Drosophila
questions.explanation: Mendel published in 1865, his work was rediscovered in 1900, Sutton and Boveri put forward the chromosomal theory in 1902, and Morgan experimentally verified linkage soon after.
questions.ncertEvidence: Principles of Inheritance and Variation, introduction and historical context sections regarding Mendel, rediscovery, and chromosomal theory.

questions.question:
What is the correct sequence of meiotic events that leads to non-disjunction and subsequent aneuploidy like Klinefelter's syndrome ($44 + XXY$)?
1. DNA replication and normal preparation for meiosis
2. Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to segregate properly during anaphase
3. Formation of abnormal gametes containing either XX or XY or lack of sex chromosomes
4. Fertilization of an abnormal gamete (e.g., $XY$) with a normal gamete (e.g., $X$)
questions.explanation: Aneuploidy results from normal pre-meiotic replication, followed by non-disjunction during anaphase, production of abnormal gametes, and subsequent fertilization resulting in chromosomal syndromes.
questions.ncertEvidence: Principles of Inheritance and Variation, Section on Genetic Disorders and Aneuploidy, explaining non-disjunction during cell division.

questions.question: Mendel's work remained unrecognized till 1900 due to several reasons. Which of the following stands as an exception or major departure from the general acceptance of his work during that period?
options: Lack of continuous variation in traits he studied
The concept of particulate inheritance proposed by him
Use of statistical logic and mathematical analysis for biology problems
Discovery of multiple alleles in natural populations
questions.explanation: Mendel's approach of using mathematics and statistics to explain biological phenomena was totally new and unacceptable to the biologists of his time, as it was considered far ahead of its time. The other options were either part of his findings or later discoveries.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 69: 'His approach of using mathematics to explain biological phenomena was totally new and unacceptable to many of the biologists of his time.'

questions.question: In a typical monohybrid cross of Mendel, the phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation is 3:1. However, which of the following known crosses represents an exception where the phenotypic ratio deviates to 1:2:1 in incomplete dominance?
options: Cross between true-breeding tall and dwarf pea plants
Cross between red-flowered and white-flowered snapdragon plants
Cross between yellow-round and green-wrinkled pea seeds
Cross between pure-breeding axial and terminal flower pea plants
questions.explanation: In snapdragon (Antirrhinum majus), the cross between true-breeding red (RR) and white (rr) flowers produces pink (Rr) flowers in F1, leading to a phenotypic ratio of 1 (red) : 2 (pink) : 1 (white) in F2, which deviates from Mendel's monohybrid ratio.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 72: 'In a cross between true-breeding red-flowered (RR) and true-breeding white-flowered plants (rr), the F1 (Rr) was pink... F2 ratio is 1 (RR) : 2 (Rr) : 1 (rr).'

questions.question: ABO blood grouping in humans is controlled by the gene I, which has three alleles (IA, IB, and i). This system elegantly demonstrates codominance. Which of the following observations specifically proves codominance rather than incomplete dominance?
options: Alleles IA and IB produce a totally new intermediate sugar polymer on RBC surface
Both IA and IB are expressed equally and independently in individuals with genotype IAIB
Allele i does not produce any sugar, acting as a recessive allele
Individuals with IAi genotype express only blood type A
questions.explanation: Codominance is demonstrated when both alleles (IA and IB) are expressed side by side without blending, producing both types of sugar polymers on the red blood cell surface in AB blood type individuals.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 73: 'When IA and IB are present together they both express their own types of sugars: this is because of codominance.'

questions.question: Starch synthesis in pea seeds is controlled by a single gene with two alleles (B and b). Homozygous large starch grain producers (BB) and homozygous small starch grain producers (bb) show an exception to standard monohybrid dominance when analyzed for seed shape. What is the phenotypic outcome in starch grain size for heterozygotes (Bb)?
options: Equal proportion of large and small starch grains
questions.explanation: For starch grain size, the gene shows incomplete dominance where heterozygotes (Bb) produce intermediate-sized starch grains, even though the same gene shows dominance for round seed shape over wrinkled seed shape.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 74: 'If starch grain size is considered as the phenotype, then from this angle, the alleles show incomplete dominance.'

questions.question: Morgan carried out several dihybrid crosses in Drosophila to study genes that were linked. In his cross between yellow-bodied, white-eyed females and brown-bodied, red-eyed males, what notable exception was observed in the F2 generation compared to Mendel's dihybrid cross results?
options: The parental combinations reappeared in significantly higher proportions than non-parental types
Independent assortment ratio of 9:3:3:1 was strictly maintained
No recombinant types were produced at all
Recessive traits completely disappeared in the F1 generation
questions.explanation: When genes are linked on the same chromosome, Morgan observed that the proportion of parental gene combinations was much higher than the non-parental (recombinant) types, sharply deviating from Mendel's independent assortment.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 77: 'Morgan attributed this due to the physical association or linkage of the two genes and coined the term linkage...'

questions.question: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inborn error of metabolism that exemplifies pleiotropy in humans. Which of the following correctly describes the exceptional nature of pleiotropic genes?
options: Multiple genes combine to influence a single phenotype
A single gene exhibits multiple phenotypic expressions
A single allele suppresses the expression of multiple unrelated genes
Alleles mutate continuously to produce multiple new species
questions.explanation: Pleiotropy occurs when a single gene mutation affects multiple phenotypic traits. In PKU, the defective enzyme causes mental retardation, reduced hair and skin pigmentation.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 74: 'The pleiotropic gene in humans causes phenylketonuria... characterized by mental retardation as well as a reduction in hair and skin pigmentation.'

questions.question: Human skin colour is controlled by polygenic inheritance, involving three genes (A, B, and C). How does polygenic inheritance distinctly contrast with Mendelian monogenic inheritance?
options: It takes into account the environmental influence exclusively
It involves multiple genes controlling a single trait with continuous variation
It shows discrete phenotypic categories without intermediates
It violates the law of segregation entirely
questions.explanation: Polygenic inheritance involves traits controlled by three or more genes, producing a spectrum of continuous variations (like human skin color), unlike single-gene Mendelian traits which show clear-cut discrete categories.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 75: 'Polygenic inheritance generally takes into account the interaction of multiple genes with continuous variation of the phenotype.'

questions.question: Chromosomal theory of inheritance proposed by Sutton and Boveri mapped the behavior of chromosomes parallel to the behavior of genes. Which of the following represents an exception where chromosome behavior does not strictly follow independent segregation?
options: Homologous chromosomes separate during anaphase I
Allele pairs segregate independently during gamete formation
Linked genes present on the same chromosome travel together
Two alleles of a gene pair are located on homologous sites
questions.explanation: While independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes, genes located on the same chromosome (linked genes) do not assort independently, which is an exception noted during linkage studies.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 76-77: 'When two genes in a dihybrid cross were situated on the same chromosome, the proportion of parental gene combinations were much higher than the non-parental type.'

questions.question: In honeybees, sex determination follows the haplo-diploid method. What is a unique exception or characteristic feature of male honeybees (drones) produced by this system?
options: They develop from fertilized eggs and have 32 chromosomes
They develop by parthenogenesis from unfertilized eggs and are haploid
They receive half of their chromosomes from a male parent and half from a female parent
They are sterile and do not produce sperm
questions.explanation: In haplo-diploid sex determination, males (drones) develop from unfertilized eggs via parthenogenesis and are haploid (n = 16 in honeybees), meaning they have fathers and grandfathers but no sons or fathers.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 83: 'The males do not have a father and thus cannot have sons, but have a grandfather and can have grandsons.'

questions.question: Pedigree analysis is a tool used to trace inheritance of specific traits through generations. Which of the following is a classic autosomal recessive pedigree exception or feature that distinguishes it from autosomal dominant disorders?
options: The trait transmits from unaffected carrier parents to affected offspring
The trait appears in every single generation without skipping
Affected individuals always have at least one affected parent
Unrelated mating frequently increases dominant trait expression
questions.explanation: Autosomal recessive traits (like sickle-cell anaemia) often skip generations and can manifest in offspring born to unaffected heterozygous carrier parents (e.g., in a typical pedigree).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, page 84-85: Pedigree analysis diagrams and text showing autosomal recessive traits like sickle-cell anaemia skipping generations.

questions.question: A cross between a true-breeding red-flowered snapdragon and a true-breeding white-flowered snapdragon yields pink-flowered plants in the F1 generation. When these F1 plants are self-pollinated, the phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation is:
questions.explanation: In Snapdragon (Antirrhinum majus), flower color shows incomplete dominance. The F2 phenotypic ratio is 1 Red : 2 Pink : 1 White, which coincides with its genotypic ratio.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 72: 'In a cross between true-breeding red-flowered (RR) and true-breeding white-flowered plants (rr), the F1 (Rr) was pink... The F2 generation gave a ratio of 1 red (RR) : 2 pink (Rr) : 1 white (rr).'

questions.question: In Drosophila, the cross of an F1 female backcrossed to a homozygous recessive male for body color and eye color shows recombinant frequencies significantly lower than 50%. This phenomenon is best explained by:
options: Physical linkage of genes on the same chromosome
questions.explanation: T.H. Morgan observed that two genes did not segregate independently of each other and the F2 ratio deviated significantly from the 9:3:3:1 ratio due to physical association or linkage of genes on the same chromosome.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 79: 'Morgan hybridized Drosophila females yellow-bodied, white-eyed to brown-bodied, red-eyed males and intercrossed their F1 progeny... genes were located on the X chromosome and 'linked'.'

questions.question: Select the correct chromosomal complement found in an individual affected with Turner's syndrome:
questions.explanation: Turner's syndrome is caused by the absence of one of the X chromosomes, resulting in a karyotype of 45 with XO. Klinefelter's syndrome is 47, XXY.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 91: 'Such a disorder is caused due to absence of one of the X chromosomes, i.e., 45 with XO, such females are sterile...'

questions.question: Which of the following traits studied by Mendel in pea plants involved a recessive allele expressing axial flower position?
options: Flower position was not studied by Mendel
questions.explanation: In Mendel's experiments with garden peas, axial flower position is the dominant trait, while terminal flower position is the recessive trait.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Table 5.1, Page 70: Characters studied by Mendel: Flower position - Axial (Dominant) / Terminal (Recessive).

questions.question: What is the genetic mechanism responsible for the ABO blood grouping system in human populations?
questions.explanation: ABO blood groups are controlled by gene I which has three alleles (IA, IB, i), representing multiple allelism. When both IA and IB are present together, they both express their own types of sugars, showing co-dominance.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 74: 'The gene (I) controls the ABO blood grouping... The alleles IA and IB produce a slightly different form of the sugar while allele i doesn't produce any sugar... when IA and IB are present together they both express their own types of sugars: this is co-dominance.'

questions.question: A genetic disorder where a single defective gene affects multiple phenotypic traits, such as phenylketonuria leading to mental retardation and reduced hair/skin pigmentation, is an example of:
questions.explanation: Pleiotropy occurs when a single gene exhibits multiple phenotypic expressions. Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a classic example where mutation of the gene coding for phenylalanine hydroxylase results in mental retardation and reduction in hair and skin pigmentation.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 75: 'The pleiotropic gene is seen in some cases where a single gene can exhibit multiple phenotypic expression. For example, phenylketonuria...'

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is an example of a chromosomal disorder caused by trisomy of an autosome?
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder resulting from the gain of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21). Turner's and Klinefelter's are sex-chromosome disorders, and Haemophilia is a Mendelian sex-linked recessive disorder.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 90: 'Down's syndrome... The cause of this genetic disorder is the presence of an additional copy of the chromosome number 21 (trisomy of 21).'

questions.question: In a typical Mendelian monohybrid cross between a homozygous tall and a homozygous dwarf pea plant, the proportion of heterozygous tall plants in the F2 generation is:
questions.explanation: In the F2 generation of a monohybrid cross, the genotypic ratio is 1 Homozygous Tall (TT) : 2 Heterozygous Tall (Tt) : 1 Homozygous Dwarf (tt). Therefore, the fraction of heterozygous tall plants is 2/4, which simplifies to 1/2.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 73: 'The 1:2:1 ratio is mathematically condensable to the form of the binomial expression (ax + by)2... [1/4 TT + 2/4 Tt + 1/4 tt].'

questions.question: What is the primary reason why female Drosophila show a lower recombination frequency between genes when compared to linked genes in male Drosophila?
options: Crossing over does not occur at all in male Drosophila
Genes are located on autosomes in males
questions.explanation: A unique feature of Drosophila genetics highlighted by Morgan and his group is that crossing over does not occur in male Drosophila, resulting in complete linkage in males.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 80: 'Morgan and his group also found that even when genes were grouped on the same chromosome, some genes were very tightly linked (showed very low recombination) while others were loosely linked (showed higher recombination)... (Note: Crossing over is absent in male Drosophila).'

questions.question: Pedigree analysis of a specific trait shows that it occurs in every generation, affects males and females equally, and an affected parent transmits it to approximately half of their offspring regardless of sex. This inheritance pattern is typically:
questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant traits do not skip generations, affect males and females equally, and can be transmitted by an affected heterozygous parent to about 50% of the offspring.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 88: 'The inheritance pattern of a autosomal dominant trait can be traced by pedigree analysis... e.g., Myotonic dystrophy.'

questions.question: Select the incorrect statement regarding Mendel's laws of inheritance.
options: The Law of Segregation is based on the fact that the alleles do not show any blending and that both the characters are recovered as such in F2 generation though one of these is not seen at the F1 stage.
The Law of Dominance is used to explain the expression of only one of the parental characters in a monohybrid cross in the F1 and the expression of both in the F2.
The Law of Segregation is universally applicable and holds true for all organisms without any exception.
The discrete unit controlling a particular character is called a factor, which now is called a gene.
questions.explanation: The Law of Dominance explains the expression of only one of the parental characters in a monohybrid cross in the F1 generation and the expression of BOTH in the F2 generation is incorrect because F2 generation shows both parental traits (in 3:1 phenotypic ratio), but the statement incorrectly implies dominance explains both in F2 in a misleading way. Wait, actually, Law of Dominance explains why only one trait appears in F1 and both appear in F2? No, Law of Segregation explains that alleles segregate so that gametes receive only one allele. Let's check NCERT: 'The law of dominance is used to explain the expression of only one of the parental characters in a monohybrid cross in the F1 and the expression of both in the F2-it is through the parental characters being expressed in F2... wait, let's look at Law of Segregation: 'The segregation of alleles is a random process and so there is a 50 percent chance of a gamete containing either allele...' Let's refine option 2: Law of Dominance explains why only one parental trait is seen in F1, but both are expressed in F2 is actually correct according to NCERT text. Let's check option 2 vs option 2 in NCERT: 'The law of dominance is used to explain the expression of only one of the parental characters in a monohybrid cross in the F1 and the expression of both in the F2-it is through the expression of traits in F2 that both characters are recovered.' Wait, the Law of Segregation states that alleles do not show any blending and that both characters are recovered as such in F2 though one is not seen in F1. Therefore, Law of Segregation is the correct concept for that description, making options or statements manipulated.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 73-75: Principles of Inheritance and Variation - Law of Segregation and Law of Dominance.

questions.question: In a dihybrid cross between two heterozygotes (RrYy x RrYy), what proportion of the offspring are expected to have the recombinant phenotypes?
questions.explanation: In a standard Mendelian dihybrid cross, the phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1. The 9 represents parental combinations (round yellow and wrinkled green, or rather round yellow), 1 represents wrinkled green (parental), and the two classes of 3/16 each represent recombinant phenotypes (round green and wrinkled yellow). Thus, total recombinants = 3/16 + 3/16 = 6/16.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 76: Dihybrid cross phenotypic ratio 9:3:3:1, where 3 and 3 represent recombinants.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is an example of chromosomal aberration involving the addition of a single chromosome?
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is caused by the presence of an additional copy of chromosome number 21 (trisomy 21), which is an addition of a single chromosome (2n + 1). Turner's syndrome is monosomy (2n - 1), Klinefelter's is trisomy involving sex chromosomes (XXY), and Phenylketonuria is a Mendelian point mutation disorder.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 92: Down's syndrome is trisomy of chromosome 21.

questions.question: Identify the mismatched pair regarding sex-determination mechanisms.
questions.explanation: Human males have an X and a Y chromosome (XY) and produce two different types of gametes, making them male heterogametic, not female heterogametic. All other pairs correctly match the organism with its sex-determination system and heterogametic sex.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 83-85: Sex determination in humans, Drosophila, birds, and grasshopper.

questions.question: Thalassaemia differs from Haemophilia in that Thalassaemia is a:
options: Recessive autosomal disorder affecting globin chain synthesis
Dominant autosomal disorder affecting blood coagulation
questions.explanation: Thalassaemia is an autosome-linked recessive disease transmitted from parents to offspring when both partners are unaffected carriers (heterozygous). It results in reduced rate of synthesis of one of the globin chains of haemoglobin. Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive disease.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 90-91: Thalassaemia and Haemophilia comparison.

questions.question: In Morgan's experiments on Drosophila, what did he observe concerning linkage and recombination?
options: Genes located on the same chromosome are always tightly linked and never show recombination.
Tightly linked genes show very high frequency of recombination.
Loosely linked genes on the same chromosome show lower recombination frequency than tightly linked genes.
Genes located on the same chromosome show physical association or linkage, and the strength of linkage depends on the distance between genes.
questions.explanation: Morgan hybridized yellow-bodied, white-eyed females to brown-bodied, red-eyed males and intercrossed their F1 progeny. He observed that two genes did not segregate independently of each other and F2 ratio deviated significantly from 9:3:3:1. Genes on the same chromosome are linked, and physical distance determines recombination frequency (closer genes = strong linkage = low recombination).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 78-79: Linkage and Recombination discovered by T.H. Morgan.

questions.question: Pedigree analysis is a strong tool utilized to study inheritance patterns. In a pedigree chart, a filled square symbol represents:
questions.explanation: In standard pedigree analysis symbols used in human genetics, squares represent males, circles represent females, and shading or filling of the symbol indicates the affected individual. Therefore, a filled square represents an affected male.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 88: Pedigree Analysis symbols (Figure 5.14).

questions.question: A cross between a homozygous tall plant with red flowers and a dwarf plant with white flowers yields F1 plants that are all tall with pink flowers. Selfing of F1 gives four phenotypes in F2. This illustrates:
options: Both independent assortment and incomplete dominance
questions.explanation: The plant height trait follows standard Mendelian independent assortment (tall is dominant over dwarf), while the flower color trait shows incomplete dominance (red crossed with white gives pink). Therefore, both independent assortment (across loci) and incomplete dominance (at the flower color locus) are operating.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 74-76: Incomplete dominance and Dihybrid cross/Law of Independent Assortment.

questions.question: Select the correct statement regarding sickle-cell anaemia.
options: It is caused by a substitution of Valine by Glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta globin chain of haemoglobin.
The mutant haemoglobin molecule undergoes polymerisation under low oxygen tension causing the change in RBC shape.
It is an X-linked dominant trait.
The affected individuals have normal resistance to malaria compared to carriers.
questions.explanation: Sickle-cell anaemia is caused by the substitution of Glutamic acid (Glu) by Valine (Val) at the sixth position of the beta globin chain. Due to this, mutant haemoglobin molecule undergoes polymerisation under low oxygen tension causing the change in RBC shape from biconcave disc to elongated sickle-like. It is autosomal recessive.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 89-90: Sickle-cell anaemia.

questions.question: What is the genetic basis of ABO blood grouping in human populations?
options: Controlled by multiple alleles where an individual possesses more than two alleles for the trait.
Controlled by a single gene with three alleles (IA, IB, i) out of which any two are inherited by an individual.
Controlled by codominance alone without any dominant-recessive relationship.
Controlled by polygenic inheritance involving five different loci.
questions.explanation: ABO blood groups are controlled by the gene I. The gene has three alleles—IA, IB, and i. Because any person has only two of these three alleles, it is an example of multiple alleles, but an individual diploid organism only carries two alleles.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 75-76: Multiple Alleles and ABO blood grouping in humans.

questions.question: A true-breeding tall pea plant is crossed with a true-breeding dwarf pea plant. The F1 generation is self-crossed. Out of 800 individuals produced in the F2 generation, how many are expected to exhibit the homozygous tall genotype based on Mendelian principles?
questions.explanation: In a monohybrid cross, the F2 genotypic ratio is 1 homozygous tall (TT) : 2 heterozygous tall (Tt) : 1 homozygous dwarf (tt). Out of 4 parts total, the homozygous tall fraction is 1/4. Therefore, 1/4 of 800 = 200 individuals.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 72: Inheritance of One Gene - Monohybrid cross genotypic ratio is 1:2:1 for TT:Tt:tt.

questions.question: In a certain plant species, flower color exhibits incomplete dominance. When a homozygous red-flowered plant (RR) is crossed with a homozygous white-flowered plant (rr), pink-flowered plants (Rr) are obtained in the F1 generation. If an F1 pink plant is test-crossed, what will be the phenotypic ratio in the progeny?
questions.explanation: A test cross involves crossing the individual with the recessive parent (rr). Crossing the F1 pink plant (Rr) with the recessive white plant (rr) yields 1 Rr (pink) : 1 rr (white), resulting in a 1:1 phenotypic ratio of pink to white.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 75: Incomplete Dominance - Crossing F1 (Rr) with recessive parent (rr) gives 1 Pink : 1 White.

questions.question: A man with blood group AB marries a woman with blood group O. Their children can potentially exhibit how many different blood group phenotypes and genotypes, respectively?
questions.explanation: A man with blood group AB has the genotype $I^A I^B$ and produces $I^A$ and $I^B$ gametes. A woman with blood group O has genotype i i and produces i gametes. The offspring genotypes will be $I^A i$ (Blood group A) and $I^B i$ (Blood group B). Thus, there are 2 phenotypes (A and B) and 2 genotypes ($I^A i$ and $I^B i$).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 75-76: Codominance and Multiple Alleles - ABO blood typing inheritance patterns.

questions.question: In Drosophila, grey body color (G) is dominant to black body color (g), and long wings (L) are dominant to vestigial wings (l). If a dihybrid female (GgLl) is test-crossed and the resulting progeny shows 41% parental types and 9% recombinant types, what is the distance between the two genes in centiMorgans (cM)?
questions.explanation: Recombination frequency is calculated as the percentage of recombinant progeny out of the total progeny. Here, the recombinant frequency is given directly as 9%. The distance between genes in map units (centiMorgans) is equal to the recombination percentage, which is 9 cM.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 78-79: Linkage and Recombination - Recombination frequency is directly proportional to the distance between genes.

questions.question: A colorblind female marries a normal vision male. What percentage of their sons are expected to be colorblind?
questions.explanation: Colorblindness is an X-linked recessive trait. A colorblind female has the genotype $X^c X^c$ and will pass an X-linked recessive allele ($X^c$) to all her sons. Since sons inherit their single X chromosome from their mother, 100% of the sons will be colorblind ($X^c Y$).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 85: Pedigree Analysis / Sex-linked inheritance - Daughters of colorblind males/females and maternal inheritance of X chromosome to sons.

questions.question: A couple has four children: three daughters and one son. The son is affected by an autosomal recessive genetic disorder, while the parents and daughters are phenotypically normal. What is the probability that their next child will be a daughter who is a carrier for the disorder?
questions.explanation: Since an affected child (autosomal recessive, 'aa') was born to normal parents, both parents must be carriers ('Aa'). For any future pregnancy, the probability of having a female child is 1/2, and the probability of that child being a carrier ('Aa') is 1/2. Therefore, the combined probability = (1/2) * (1/2) = 1/4.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 83: Pedigree Analysis and Mendelian disorders - Autosomal recessive transmission probability.

questions.question: Which of the following chromosomal aberrations correctly describes the genetic basis of Down's syndrome?
options: Trisomy of the X chromosome ($47, XXX$)
Deletion of short arm of chromosome 5
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder caused by the presence of an additional copy of chromosome 21, resulting in trisomy (47 chromosomes).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 87: Chromosomal Disorders - Down's Syndrome is due to trisomy of chromosome 21.

questions.question: In a pedigree chart, a diamond symbol ($\diamond$) typically represents which of the following?
questions.explanation: Standard pedigree symbols used in human genetics include squares for males, circles for females, and diamonds for individuals of unspecified sex.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 83: Pedigree Analysis - Table of standard symbols used in pedigrees.

questions.question: A plant with genotype AABbCC is self-pollinated. Assuming independent assortment of all three gene loci, what proportion of the F1 progeny will be completely homozygous for all three loci?
questions.explanation: For locus A (AA x AA), 100% homozygous (AA). For locus B (Bb x Bb), 1/2 homozygous (1/4 BB + 1/4 bb). For locus C (CC x CC), 100% homozygous (CC). Total homozygous proportion = 1 * (1/2) * 1 = 1/2? Wait, let's check: Bb x Bb gives BB (1/4), Bb (1/2), bb (1/4). Homozygous fraction at B is 1/2. Locus A is 1, Locus C is 1. Product = 1 * 1/2 * 1 = 1/2.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 73-74: Principles of Inheritance and Variation - Independent assortment and probability calculations.

questions.question: A cross between a true-breeding red-flowered snapdragon (Antirrhinum majus) and a true-breeding white-flowered snapdragon yielded all pink flowers in the $F_1$ generation. When $F_1$ plants were self-pollinated, the $F_2$ generation showed phenotypic and genotypic ratios identical to 1:2:1. What inference can be drawn regarding the nature of inheritance in this case?
options: The alleles show incomplete dominance, and the $F_2$ phenotypic ratio matches the genotypic ratio because the heterozygote has a distinct intermediate phenotype.
The alleles show codominance, and the trait is controlled by multiple alleles rather than a single gene pair.
The red allele is completely dominant over the white allele, but incomplete penetrance caused pink coloration in the heterozygote.
The phenotypic ratio deviates from Mendel's monohybrid ratio because of lethal gene interactions in the homozygous dominant condition.
questions.explanation: In snapdragon (incomplete dominance), the $F_1$ generation (Rr) is pink. Selfing $F_1$ yields 1 Red (RR) : 2 Pink (Rr) : 1 White (rr), making both the phenotypic and genotypic ratios 1:2:1.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 73: 'In snapdragon... the hybrid (Rr) derived from cross between red (RR) and white (rr) flowers had pink (Rr) colour... both genotypic and phenotypic ratios would be 1:2:1.'

questions.question: A geneticist analyzes a pedigree and finds that a particular trait appears in every generation, affects males and females equally, and affected individuals have at least one affected parent. However, when an affected heterozygous male mates with an unaffected female, exactly half of their sons and half of their daughters show the trait. Which pattern of inheritance is most strongly inferred?
questions.explanation: Transmission across generations without skipping (vertical transmission), equal affection of both sexes, and a 50% recurrence risk in offspring of a heterozygote with a normal individual point strictly to autosomal dominant inheritance.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 88-89: Discussion on autosomal dominant traits such as Myotonic dystrophy and their characteristic pedigree patterns.

questions.question: In a dihybrid cross involving two linked genes located close to each other on the same chromosome, Thomas Hunt Morgan observed that the proportion of parental gene combinations in the $F_2$ generation was significantly higher than the non-parental (recombinant) types. What is the fundamental biological inference behind this observation?
options: The genes assort independently during meiosis due to random alignment at the metaphase plate.
Physical association or linkage between genes on the same chromosome prevents their complete independent assortment.
Crossing over occurs with a frequency of 100% between linked genes.
The alleles undergo mutation at a high frequency during gametogenesis.
questions.explanation: Morgan found that genes located on the same chromosome do not segregate independently in the manner of unlinked genes; physical linkage results in higher parental combinations due to the tendency of genes to stay together during inheritance.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 79-80: 'Morgan attributed this due to the physical association or linkage of the two genes and coined the term linkage...'

questions.question: A human male is found to have 47 chromosomes, including XXY sex chromosomes. He exhibits Klinefelter's syndrome, characterized by overall masculine development with feminine voice pitch and breast development (gynaecomastia). Which meiotic error during gametogenesis in the parents can be directly inferred to cause this condition?
options: Non-disjunction of autosomes during paternal meiosis I
Failure of cytokinesis during maternal mitosis
Non-disjunction of sex chromosomes either during maternal or paternal gametogenesis
Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 during embryonic cleavage
questions.explanation: Klinefelter's syndrome (47, XXY) is caused by the non-disjunction of sex chromosomes during meiosis, resulting in the fusion of an abnormal gamete containing two sex chromosomes (XX or XY) with a normal gamete.
