questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 110, Transcription in Eukaryotes: 'In capping an unusual nucleotide (methyl guanosine triphosphate) is added to the 5'-end of hnRNA. In tailing, adenylate residues (200-300) are added at 3'-end in a template independent manner.'

questions.question: Choose the incorrect statement regarding the chemical structure of polynucleotide chains from the given options.
options: A nitrogenous base is linked to the pentose sugar through an N-glycosidic linkage.
The phosphate group is linked to the 5'-OH of a nucleoside through a phosphodiester linkage.
Two nucleosides are linked through 3'-5' phosphodiester linkage to form a dinucleotide.
The backbone in a polynucleotide chain is formed due to sugar and phosphates.
questions.explanation: A phosphate group is linked to the 5'-OH of a *nucleoside* to form a *nucleotide*, not directly to another nucleoside via phosphodiester linkage; phosphodiester linkages connect adjacent nucleotides (specifically the 3'-carbon of one sugar to the 5'-carbon of the next sugar).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 5.1.1: 'A phosphate group is linked to 5'-OH of a nucleoside through phosphoester linkage...'

questions.question: Which of the following components correctly defines a nucleoside when combined?
options: Nitrogenous base + Pentose sugar + Phosphate group
questions.explanation: A nucleoside is formed when a nitrogenous base is attached to a pentose sugar (ribose or deoxyribose) through an N-glycosidic linkage. Addition of a phosphate group makes it a nucleotide.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 5.1.1: 'Adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil and thymine are nitrogenbases. ... When linked to sugar, they are called nucleosides.'

questions.question: In the DNA double helix model proposed by Watson and Crick, the two strands are said to be antiparallel. This means that:
options: one strand runs in the 5'->3' direction and the other in 3'->5' direction.
both strands run in the 5'->3' direction.
both strands run in the 3'->5' direction.
one strand is twisted clockwise and the other is twisted counter-clockwise.
questions.explanation: The two chains of DNA have antiparallel polarity, meaning if one chain has the polarity 5'->3', the other has 3'->5'.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 5.1.2: 'The two chains have anti-parallel polarity. It means, if one chain has the polarity 5'-3', the other has 3'-5'.'

questions.question: Identify the correct statement about the packaging of DNA helix in prokaryotes like E. coli.
options: Prokaryotes possess a well-defined nucleus containing histone octamers.
DNA is negatively charged and is held with positively charged proteins in a region termed nucleoid.
DNA in E. coli is wrapped around positively charged histone proteins to form nucleosomes.
Prokaryotic DNA is completely free of any proteins.
questions.explanation: In prokaryotes, DNA is not scattered throughout the cell. Though they do not have a defined nucleus, the positively charged proteins assist the negatively charged DNA to stay in a region called the nucleoid.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 5.4.1: 'Though they do not have a defined nucleus, the DNA is not scattered through the cell... DNA being negatively charged is held with some proteins (that have positive charges) in a region termed as 'nucleoid'.'

questions.question: During DNA replication in eukaryotes, replication fork is formed. Which enzyme is primarily responsible for elongation by polymerization of deoxynucleotides?
questions.explanation: DNA-dependent DNA polymerases are the main enzymes used for catalyzing polymerization of a large number of nucleotides in a very short time during DNA replication.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 5.3.1: '...DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalysts polymerization on a large number of nucleotides in a very short time.'

questions.question: Which of the following RNAs acts as both an adapter molecule and a structural molecule, and was originally known as sRNA (soluble RNA)?
questions.explanation: Transfer RNA (tRNA), previously known as sRNA (soluble RNA), acts as an adapter molecule that reads the code on mRNA and brings amino acids to the ribosome.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 5.3.3: 'tRNA—the adapter molecule... position of tRNA was as a reader (adapter) that would one-hand read and on the other hand bind to amino acids. ... previously known as sRNA (soluble RNA).'

questions.question: The process of copying genetic information from one strand of DNA into RNA is known as:
questions.explanation: Transcription is the process of copying genetic information from one strand of the DNA into RNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 5.3: 'Transcription is the process of copying genetic information from one strand of the DNA into RNA.'

questions.question: In Griffith's transforming principle experiment, virulent Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteria were:
questions.explanation: In Griffith's experiment, mice infected with the S-strain (virulent/smooth, mucus coated) died from pneumonia, whereas mice infected with the R-strain (rough, non-virulent) lived.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 5.2: 'S-strain (smooth, virulent) ... R-strain (rough, non-virulent). Mice infected with the S-strain die from pneumonia infection.'

questions.question: Which scientist(s) conclusively proved that DNA is the genetic material using bacteriophages?
questions.explanation: Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952) worked with viruses that infect bacteria (bacteriophages) and gave unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 5.2.2: 'The unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material came from the experiments of Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952).'

questions.question: What is the primary function of the lac operon in bacteria such as E. coli?
options: Catabolic pathway regulated by presence of lactose
questions.explanation: The lac operon is a catabolic operon in E. coli wherein lactose acts as the inducer that regulates the switching on and off of the operon.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 5.8 (Lac operon): 'The lac operon consists of one regulatory gene and three structural genes... it is a catabolic pathway.'

questions.question: A researcher treats a replicating DNA molecule with radioactive thymidine to trace the synthesis of daughter strands. If the replication fork moves from left to right, what will be the structural characteristic of newly synthesized strands?
options: Both strands are synthesized continuously from left to right.
One strand is synthesized continuously, while the other is synthesized discontinuously in small segments moving opposite to the fork movement.
Both strands are synthesized discontinuously in short Okazaki fragments.
The leading strand is synthesized towards the 5' end of the template while the lagging strand moves towards the 3' end.
questions.explanation: Because DNA polymerase can only catalyze polymerization in the 5' to 3' direction, replication on one template strand (leading strand) is continuous, while on the other template strand (lagging strand), it is synthesized discontinuously in short segments known as Okazaki fragments, moving in the direction opposite to the unwinding fork.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.5 - Replication: 'Consequently, replication does not initiate simultaneously in both strands. Also, one strand is replicated continuously... while the other is replicated discontinuously.'

questions.question: During transcription in a bacterial cell, the RNA polymerase enzyme encounters a terminator sequence. What is the immediate functional consequence on the transcription process?
options: RNA polymerase recognizes the promoter and initiates transcription of a structural gene.
Rho factor binds to the DNA and unwinds the double helix ahead of the enzyme.
The newly synthesized RNA molecule and the RNA polymerase enzyme are released from the DNA template.
Splicing of introns and capping of the nascent mRNA occur simultaneously.
questions.explanation: At the termination region of a transcription unit, a terminator sequence signals the end of transcription. When RNA polymerase reaches this point, the nascent RNA falls off, and the enzyme is released, terminating transcription.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.6 - Transcription: 'It is conventionally defined as the DNA sequence that codes for tRNA or rRNA molecule... The terminator defines the end of the process.'

questions.question: In an experiment, a biochemist isolates mRNA from eukaryotic cells and finds it significantly shorter than the primary transcript (hnRNA) synthesized in the nucleus. Which of the following processing events accounts for this difference?
options: Addition of adenylate residues at the 3' end (polyadenylation).
Addition of a methylated guanosine triphosphate cap at the 5' end.
Removal of non-coding introns and joining of coding exons in a defined order.
Conversion of cytosine to uracil via RNA editing enzymes.
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic genes contain split genes where coding regions (exons) are interrupted by non-coding regions (introns). During RNA splicing, introns are removed and exons are joined together, making the mature processed mRNA shorter than the initial heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.6 - Transcription (RNA Splicing): 'In splicing, the introns are removed and exons are joined in a defined order.'

questions.question: A geneticist studies a mutant strain of E. coli where the lac operon is constitutively expressed even in the complete absence of lactose (inducer). Which molecular defect in the operon components would most logically explain this phenotype?
options: A mutation in the structural gene 'z' rendering beta-galactosidase inactive.
A mutation in the operator region that prevents the repressor protein from binding.
A mutation in the promoter region preventing RNA polymerase binding.
A deletion in the structural gene 'a' coding for transacetylase.
questions.explanation: The lac operon repressor protein normally binds to the operator region to block transcription in the absence of an inducer. If a mutation alters the operator sequence such that the repressor can no longer recognize or bind to it, transcription proceeds constitutively regardless of lactose presence.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.8 - Regulation of Gene Expression: 'The repressor protein binds to the operator region of the operon and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon... In the presence of an inducer... the repressor is inactivated.'

questions.question: If the sequence of the coding strand in a transcription unit is written as 5'-ATGCAGTC-3', what will be the sequence of the corresponding transcribed mRNA?
questions.explanation: The coding strand (sense strand) has the same sequence as the RNA molecule, except that thymine (T) in DNA is replaced by uracil (U) in RNA, and both run in the 5' to 3' direction. Coding strand: 5'-ATGCAGTC-3' yields mRNA: 5'-AUGCAGUC-3'.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.6 - Transcription: 'The two strands have opposite polarity... The strand that does not code for anything is called coding strand... remember, the coding strand in a transcription unit is not translated.'

questions.question: During DNA replication, topoisomerase plays a critical mechanical role. What would happen to the replication process if topoisomerase activity were selectively inhibited?
options: Nucleotides would fail to form phosphodiester bonds due to lack of energy.
RNA primers would not be removed from the lagging strand.
Supercoiling tension ahead of the replication fork would cause DNA breakage and halt unwinding.
Complementary base pairing between incoming dNTPs and template strands would fail.
questions.explanation: As DNA helicase unwinds the double helix during replication, torsional strain builds up, creating increased supercoiling ahead of the replication fork. Topoisomerase enzymes relieve this topological stress by nicking and re-joining DNA strands.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.5 - Replication: Discusses the enzymatic machinery required for unwinding and replicating DNA without mechanical obstruction.

questions.question: An analysis of DNA from a newly discovered extremophile bacterium reveals that 38% of its nitrogenous bases are Cytosine. According to Chargaff's rules, what percentage of Adenine would be present in this organism's DNA?
questions.explanation: According to Chargaff's rules for double-stranded DNA, the amount of adenine equals thymine (%A = %T) and the amount of cytosine equals guanine (%C = %G). If Cytosine is 38%, Guanine is also 38%, totaling 76% (C+G). The remaining percentage for Adenine and Thymine is 100% - 76% = 24%. Since A = T, Adenine is 24% / 2 = 12%.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.1.2 - The Search for Genetic Material / Salient features of double-helix: 'Chargaff's rules stated that for a double stranded DNA, the ratios between Adenine and Thymine and Guanine and Cytosine are constant and equals one.'

questions.question: A eukaryotic gene contains an exon-intron junction mutation that prevents correct spliceosome recognition. How will this directly impact the final protein product synthesized?
options: Translation will initiate from the wrong start codon.
The amino acid sequence may be altered due to reading frame shifts or inclusion of intronic sequences.
Transcription will prematurely terminate at the mutated junction site.
Ribosomes will fail to attach to the 5' cap of the mRNA.
questions.explanation: If a splice site mutation occurs, introns may fail to be removed or exons may be improperly excised, leading to aberrant mRNA. When translated, this abnormal mRNA can result in a shift in the reading frame or inclusion of non-coding intron amino acid stretches, altering the protein.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.6 - Transcription: 'The presence of introns is reminiscent of antiquity, and the process of splicing represents the dominance of RNA-world.'

questions.question: Which of the following experimental observations by Hershey and Chase definitively proved that DNA, and not protein, is the genetic material in bacteriophage T2?
options: Radioactive sulfur ($^{35}S$) was found inside the infected bacterial cells.
Radioactive phosphorus ($^{32}P$) was detected in the supernatant after centrifugation.
Progeny phages produced inside the bacteria contained radioactive phosphorus ($^{32}P$).
Non-radioactive protein coats entered the bacterial cytoplasm during infection.
questions.explanation: In the Hershey-Chase experiment, phages grown with radioactive phosphorus ($^{32}P$) labeled their DNA. When these phages infected bacteria, the $^{32}P$-labeled DNA entered the cells, and subsequent progeny phages contained radioactive phosphorus, proving DNA carried genetic information.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.2 - The Genetic Material: 'The bacteria which were infected with viruses that had radioactive DNA were radioactive... indicating that DNA was the material that passed from the virus to the bacteria.'

questions.question: Why is RNA considered more labile and prone to mutation compared to DNA as a genetic material?
options: The presence of a 2'-OH group on every nucleotide ribose sugar makes RNA catalytic and reactive.
RNA lacks uracil, which is more stable than thymine in cellular environments.
RNA is strictly single-stranded and lacks any complementary base-pairing capabilities.
RNA polymerase lacks any proofreading mechanisms during transcription.
questions.explanation: The 2'-OH group present at every nucleotide in RNA is a reactive functional group that makes RNA labile and easily degradable. This reactive hydroxyl group also makes RNA catalytic, unlike the chemically stable deoxyribose sugar in DNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.2.2 - RNA World: 'A-2' hydroxyl group present at every nucleotide in RNA is a reactive group and makes RNA labile and easily degradable. RNA is also now known to be catalytic, hence reactive.'

questions.question: If a double-stranded DNA molecule has 20% cytosine bases, what will be the percentage of adenine bases according to Chargaff's rules?
questions.explanation: According to Chargaff's rules, the amount of cytosine is equal to guanine (C = G = 20%), and the amount of adenine is equal to thymine (A = T). Since C + G = 40%, the remaining 60% must be A + T. Therefore, adenine (A) is 60% / 2 = 30%.
questions.ncertEvidence: Chargaff's rules state that for a double stranded DNA, the ratios between Adenine and Thymine and Guanine and Cytosine are constant and equals one (A=T and C=G).

questions.question: During DNA replication, RNA primers are required because:
options: DNA polymerase can initiate replication de novo without any preexisting strand.
DNA polymerase requires a free 3'-OH group already present on a nucleotide to add subsequent nucleotides.
RNA primers provide the necessary high-energy phosphate bonds for ligation.
Primase acts as the primary proofreading enzyme before DNA polymerase binds.
questions.explanation: DNA polymerases are unable to initiate synthesis of a DNA strand de novo; they can only add nucleotides to a pre-existing strand having a free 3'-OH group. RNA primers synthesized by primase provide this starting 3'-OH.
questions.ncertEvidence: DNA polymerases on their own cannot initiate the process of replication and need a free 3'-OH group.

questions.question: An organism is found to have its genetic material as single-stranded RNA where the percentage of Uracil is 30% and Adenine is 20%. Can this RNA be considered as double-stranded?
options: Yes, because Uracil pairs with Adenine.
No, because A does not equal U and C does not equal G in single-stranded nucleic acids.
No, because RNA never contains Uracil in equal amounts to Adenine.
questions.explanation: Chargaff's equivalence rule (A=T and C=G) applies specifically to double-stranded DNA. In single-stranded nucleic acids (like single-stranded RNA or DNA), base ratios like A=U or C=G do not necessarily hold true.
questions.ncertEvidence: Chargaff's rules stating A=T and C=G are applicable to double-stranded DNA structures.

questions.question: In Griffith's transformation experiment, which of the following treatments of heat-killed S-strain bacteria would still result in the death of mice when injected along with live R-strain bacteria?
options: Treating with both DNase and Proteases
questions.explanation: Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty discovered that DNA is the transforming principle. Treating heat-killed S-strain with RNase or proteases did not destroy the transforming ability, whereas DNase did. Thus, RNase treatment leaves the transforming DNA intact, allowing transformation to occur.
questions.ncertEvidence: Avery et al. demonstrated that digestion with protein and RNA did not affect transformation, whereas DNase did, proving DNA is the hereditary material.

questions.question: If the coding strand of a transcription unit has the sequence 5'-ATGCAG-3', what will be the sequence of the resulting mRNA transcribed from this DNA?
questions.explanation: The mRNA sequence is identical to the coding strand (except thymine is replaced by uracil). Since the coding strand is 5'-ATGCAG-3', the mRNA sequence will be 5'-AUGCAG-3'.
questions.ncertEvidence: The strand with polarity 3'->5' acts as the template, and the sequence of the coding strand (5'->3') is identical to the transcribed mRNA except T is replaced by U.

questions.question: Why is the template strand oriented in the 3'->5' direction during transcription?
options: RNA polymerase requires a 5'->3' template to synthesize in the same direction.
RNA polymerase catalyzes polymerization exclusively in the 5'->3' direction.
The promoter is always located at the 5' end of the template strand.
It prevents premature termination by rho factor.
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase, like DNA polymerase, performs polymerization only in one direction, which is 5' to 3'. Consequently, it must read the template strand in the 3' to 5' direction.
questions.ncertEvidence: RNA polymerase facilitates polymerization in only one direction, that is, 5'->3'.

questions.question: In the lac operon, if a mutation occurs in the regulator gene ('i') that produces a non-functional repressor protein, what will be the phenotypic expression of structural operon genes in the absence of an inducer (lactose)?
options: Expressed only in the presence of glucose
questions.explanation: The regulator gene codes for the repressor. A non-functional repressor cannot bind to the operator region. Therefore, the operator is never blocked, leading to constitutive (continuous) expression of the structural genes even without the inducer (lactose).
questions.ncertEvidence: In the absence of inducer, the repressor binds to the operator and silences transcription. A mutant repressor that fails to bind operator leads to constitutive transcription.

questions.question: During translation, the formation of a peptide bond between adjacent amino acids is catalyzed by:
questions.explanation: In bacteria, the 23S rRNA acts as a ribozyme (peptidyl transferase) to catalyze peptide bond formation between amino acids, demonstrating that RNA can act as an enzyme.
questions.ncertEvidence: In bacteria, 23S rRNA acts as a ribozyme for peptide bond formation.

questions.question: What is the primary function of hnRNA processing (splicing, capping, and tailing) in eukaryotes?
options: To transport mRNA out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm.
To remove non-coding introns and join exons, and protect mRNA from degradation.
To increase the rate of transcription by RNA polymerase II.
To attach ribosomes to the mRNA transcript.
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic transcripts contain non-functional introns that are removed by splicing, while exons are joined. Capping (5') and tailing (polyadenylation at 3') protect the mRNA from enzymatic degradation in the cytoplasm.
questions.ncertEvidence: Splicing removes introns and joins exons in a defined way. Capping and tailing protect RNA from degradation.

questions.question: Meselson and Stahl used 15N to prove semi-conservative DNA replication. After two generations of replication in a 14N medium, what proportion of DNA molecules are expected to be of hybrid density (15N-14N)?
questions.explanation: Starting with completely heavy DNA (15N-15N) and growing for two generations in 14N: Generation 1 yields 100% hybrid (15N-14N) DNA. Generation 2 yields 50% hybrid DNA and 50% light (14N-14N) DNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: Meselson and Stahl experiment showed that after two generations in 14N medium, 50 percent DNA is hybrid and 50 percent is light.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the enzyme responsible for relieving the strain caused by uncoiling of DNA during replication?
questions.explanation: Topoisomerase releases the torsional strain that develops ahead of the replication fork due to the uncoiling of DNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, mechanism of DNA replication.

questions.question: Identify the process in which RNA is synthesized using a DNA template strand, requiring RNA polymerase.
questions.explanation: Transcription is the process of copying genetic information from one strand of the DNA into RNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Transcription section.

questions.question: Which structural component is shared by both DNA and RNA nucleotides?
questions.explanation: Both DNA and RNA nucleotides consist of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, The DNA structure.

questions.question: During translation, which molecule acts as an adapter, carrying amino acids and reading the genetic code on mRNA?
questions.explanation: tRNA (transfer RNA) was postulated to have an adapter molecule that would read the code on one hand and bind to specific amino acids on the other.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Translation section.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the lac operon's 'i' gene?
options: It codes for the repressor protein
questions.explanation: The 'i' gene in the lac operon codes for the repressor of the operon.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Lac Operon.

questions.question: Which nitrogenous base is present in DNA instead of uracil found in RNA?
questions.explanation: DNA contains thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Structure of Polynucleotide Chain.

questions.question: In the Meselson and Stahl experiment, heavy DNA (${}^{15}	ext{N}$) was distinguished from normal DNA (${}^{14}	ext{N}$) by centrifugation in which gradient?
questions.explanation: Meselson and Stahl used cesium chloride ($	ext{CsCl}$) density gradient centrifugation to measure the densities of DNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, The Experimental Proof.

questions.question: What defines the template strand polarity for DNA-dependent RNA polymerase during transcription?
questions.explanation: The DNA strand with 3'->5' polarity acts as a template for RNA polymerase to catalyze polymerization in the 5'->3' direction.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Transcription Unit.

questions.question: What is the term for segments of coding sequences separated by non-coding introns in eukaryotic split genes?
questions.explanation: Exons are the coding sequences or expressed sequences that appear in mature or processed RNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Transcription in Eukaryotes.

questions.question: Which enzyme is responsible for joining Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand during DNA replication?
questions.explanation: DNA ligase joins the discontinuously synthesized Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, The Machinery and the Enzymes.

questions.question: Identify the incorrect statement regarding the salient features of the double-helix structure of DNA, and thus eliminate it.
options: The two chains have anti-parallel polarity.
The back-bone is constituted by sugar-phosphate and bases project inside.
The plane of one base pair stacks over the other in double helix and confers stability.
The adenine forms three hydrogen bonds with thymine, and cytosine forms two hydrogen bonds with guanine.
questions.explanation: Adenine forms two hydrogen bonds with thymine from the opposite strand, and cytosine forms three hydrogen bonds with guanine. Thus, the statement claiming adenine forms three bonds and cytosine two is incorrect.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 109: 'Adenine forms two hydrogen bonds with Thymine from the opposite strand and vice-versa. Similarly, Guanine is bonded with Cytosine with three H-bonds.'

questions.question: Which of the following properties is NOT exhibited by genetic material according to the criteria given in molecular biology?
options: It should be able to generate its replica.
It should be chemically and structurally unstable to facilitate rapid mutations.
It should provide the scope for slow changes (mutations) that are required for evolution.
It should be able to express itself in the form of 'Mendelian characters'.
questions.explanation: Genetic material must be chemically and structurally stable; instability would lead to degradation and loss of genetic information. It requires mutational stability, not instability, though it should allow slow mutations for evolution.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 113: 'It should be chemically and structurally stable... stability is one of the properties of genetic material.'

questions.question: Analyze the steps of translation and eliminate the option that does not correctly describe the mechanism of protein synthesis.
options: Charging of tRNA involves activation of amino acids in the presence of ATP and linking to their cognate tRNA.
The cellular factory for protein synthesis is the ribosome.
Peptide bond formation between adjacent amino acids requires an external ATP source.
The ribosome consists of structural RNAs and about 80 different proteins.
questions.explanation: The formation of a peptide bond does not directly require an external ATP source; the energy is derived from the charged tRNA (aminoacyl-tRNA) formation step where ATP is consumed earlier.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 117: 'The ribosome also acts as a catalyst... for the formation of peptide bond' and charging of tRNA requires ATP.

questions.question: Consider the characteristics of the Lac operon and eliminate the incorrect statement among the following:
options: The y gene codes for permease, which increases permeability of the cell to $\beta$-galactosides.
The i gene codes for the repressor of the operon.
The lactose acts as the inducer that binds to the repressor and inactivates it.
The z gene codes for transacetylase which transfers an acetyl group to $\beta$-galactoside.
questions.explanation: The z gene codes for $\beta$-galactosidase, not transacetylase. Transacetylase is coded by the a gene.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 118: 'the z gene codes for beta-galactosidase... the y gene codes for permease... the a gene encodes a transacetylase.'

questions.question: Examine the features of DNA replication in E. coli and eliminate the wrong assertion:
options: Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates serve dual purposes: act as substrates and provide energy for polymerization.
DNA polymerase catalyzes polymerization only in one direction, i.e., 5' -> 3'.
The lagging strand template allows continuous synthesis of DNA fragments.
questions.explanation: The lagging strand template results in discontinuous synthesis of DNA fragments (Okazaki fragments), not continuous synthesis. Continuous synthesis occurs on the leading strand.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 108 & 109: 'The replication is continuous on one strand (5'->3'), and discontinuous on the other.'

questions.question: Review the salient features of the human genome and identify the incorrect statement to eliminate it:
options: The human genome contains 3164.7 million nucleotide bases.
Less than 2 percent of the genome codes for proteins.
Chromosome 1 has the fewest genes (231 genes) and the Y chromosome has the most genes (2968 genes).
Repeated sequences make up a very large portion of the human genome.
questions.explanation: Chromosome 1 actually has the most genes (2968 genes), whereas the Y chromosome has the fewest genes (231 genes). The statement reverses this fact.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 119 & 120: 'Chromosome 1 has most genes (2968), and the y has the fewest (231).'

questions.question: Evaluate RNA world hypothesis and transcription factors, then eliminate the false statement:
options: RNA was the first genetic material.
Essential life processes such as metabolism, translation, and splicing evolved around RNA.
Because RNA is reactive and unstable, DNA evolved from RNA with chemical modifications for better stability.
The template strand during transcription has 5' to 3' polarity to allow the coding strand to run 3' to 5'.
questions.explanation: The DNA template strand runs with 3' to 5' polarity (not 5' to 3') so that transcription can proceed in the 5' to 3' direction.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 109 & 114: 'The DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyses polymerisation in only one direction, that is, 5'->3'... the strand that has the polarity 3'->5' acts as a template.'

questions.question: Identify the incorrect match regarding Hershey and Chase experiments and eliminate it:
options: Radioactive sulfur ($^{35}S$) - Labelled viral protein coat
Supernatant after centrifugation - Contained heavy bacterial cells with infected material
questions.explanation: In the centrifugation step, the heavier bacterial cells settled in the pellet, while the lighter viral coats remained in the supernatant.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 103: 'Bacteria that were infected with viruses that had radioactive DNA were radioactive... whereas bacteria that were infected with viruses that had radioactive proteins were not radioactive. The supernatant contained radioactive sulfur.'

questions.question: Look at the characteristics of genetic code and eliminate the exception or wrong statement:
options: The code is degenerate, meaning some amino acids are coded by more than one codon.
The codon is read in mRNA in a contiguous fashion without punctuations.
AUG has dual functions: it codes for Methionine and acts as an initiator codon.
UAG, UAA, and UGA are initiator codons that start protein synthesis.
questions.explanation: UAG, UAA, and UGA are stop (termination) codons, not initiator codons. AUG is the initiator codon.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 112: 'three codons---UAA, UAG, UGA---were found to be stop codons.'

questions.question: Analyze DNA fingerprinting steps and eliminate the incorrect procedural statement:
options: Isolation of DNA is the first step.
Digestion of DNA by restriction endonucleases produces identical fragment lengths for all humans.
Southern blotting involves transferring DNA fragments to synthetic membranes like nitrocellulose or nylon.
Hybridization is carried out using a labelled VNTR probe.
questions.explanation: Restriction endonuclease digestion produces fragments of varying lengths (polymorphisms) unique to every individual (except identical twins), not identical fragment lengths for all humans.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 121: 'Digestion of DNA by restriction endonucleases... fragments of differing sizes... Polymorphism in DNA sequence is the basis of genetic mapping of human genome as well as of DNA fingerprinting.'

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the polarity and direction of DNA replication on both template strands simultaneously at a replication fork?
options: Replication is always 5' to 3' on both strands, hence continuous on one and discontinuous on the other.
Replication proceeds 5' to 3' on the leading strand and 3' to 5' on the lagging strand to maintain overall bidirectional movement.
DNA polymerase synthesizes both strands in the 3' to 5' direction relative to the newly formed strands.
The leading strand is synthesized towards the replication fork discontinuously while the lagging strand is continuous.
questions.explanation: DNA polymerases can only catalyze polymerization in the 5' to 3' direction. Because the double helix is antiparallel, the replication fork allows continuous synthesis on the 3' to 5' template (leading strand) and discontinuous synthesis on the 5' to 3' template (lagging strand forming Okazaki fragments).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 108: 'Consequently, replication does not open simultaneously... because DNA polymerase-I/III can only add nucleotides in 5'->3' direction... one strand is continuous (leading), other is discontinuous (lagging).'

questions.question: During transcription in a bacterial cell, if the coding strand has the sequence 5'-ATGCAG-3', what will be the sequence of the RNA transcribed?
questions.explanation: The RNA transcript is identical in sequence to the coding strand (except thymine is replaced by uracil). Since the coding strand is 5'-ATGCAG-3', the mRNA sequence is 5'-AUGCAG-3'. Students often mistakenly transcribe the template strand instead, falling into the trap.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 109: 'The strand with the polarity 5'->3' and the sequence same as RNA (except thymine at the place of uracil) is displaced/termed as coding strand.'

questions.question: In the lac operon of E. coli, what is the exact function of the 'i' gene?
options: It codes for the repressor protein that binds to the operator region.
It codes for the inducer molecule (allolactose) which turns the operon on.
It is the structural gene that codes for beta-galactosidase.
It acts as the promoter site where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription.
questions.explanation: The 'i' gene in the lac operon stands for the inhibitor gene, which codes for the repressor protein. The inducer is lactose/allolactose (not coded by 'i'), and structural genes are z, y, and a.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 117: 'The i gene codes for the repressor of the lac operon.'

questions.question: Select the correct combination of triplet codon and its corresponding amino acid that represents a classic exception or specific feature highlighted in the genetic code table.
options: AUG codes for Methionine and also acts as an initiator codon.
UAA codes for Tryptophan under specific mitochondrial conditions.
UGG codes exclusively for Stop codon signals in eukaryotes.
AUG codes solely for chain elongation without any initiation role.
questions.explanation: AUG has dual functions: it codes for the amino acid methionine (Met) and acts as the initiator codon. The other options contain incorrect biological facts regarding standard genetic code properties.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 112: 'some codons code for more than one... AUG has dual functions. It codes for methionine (met) , and it also act as initiator codon.'

questions.question: What is the primary role of amino-acyl tRNA synthetases during protein synthesis?
options: Charging of tRNA by covalently linking it to its specific amino acid.
Forming peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids at the ribosome P-site.
Recognizing stop codons and terminating translation.
Unwinding the mRNA secondary structure prior to ribosome binding.
questions.explanation: Amino-acyl tRNA synthetases are enzymes responsible for charging tRNAs, i.e., attaching the specific amino acid to its cognate tRNA using ATP energy. Peptide bond formation is catalyzed by rRNA (ribozyme), not synthetases.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 115: 'For initiation, transport of amino acid to tRNA (charging of tRNA or aminoacylation of tRNA)... specific amino acid is activated in the presence of ATP and linked to its cognate tRNA.'

questions.question: In Griffith's transformation experiment, why did mice infected with a mixture of heat-killed Smooth (S) strain and live Rough (R) strain die of pneumonia?
options: Some 'R' strain bacteria were transformed into virulent 'S' strain by genetic material from heat-killed 'S' bacteria.
Heat-killed S strain bacteria revived inside the mouse body due to favorable temperature conditions.
Live R strain bacteria mutated spontaneously into S strain due to the toxic metabolic byproducts of heat-killed S bacteria.
The immune system of the mouse was weakened exclusively by the heat shock proteins released from the S strain.
questions.explanation: Griffith observed that mice died when injected with live R strain plus heat-killed S strain because the live R bacteria underwent transformation, acquiring the genetic material (DNA) for capsule formation from the dead S bacteria.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 102-103: 'This must be due to the transfer of the genetic material... live R strain of bacteria had somehow been transformed by the heat-killed S strain bacteria.'

questions.question: During DNA fingerprinting using VNTRs (Variable Number of Tandem Repeats), what does the term 'hybridization' refer to?
options: Binding of labelled VNTR probes to complementary DNA sequences on the nitrocellulose membrane.
Joining of Okazaki fragments by DNA ligase during genomic extraction.
Annealing of primers during PCR amplification of genomic DNA.
The cross-breeding between different human ethnic groups to analyze polymorphism.
questions.explanation: In DNA fingerprinting, after Southern blotting, a radioactive DNA probe (VNTR probe) is allowed to bind to its complementary target sequence immobilized on the membrane, a process termed hybridization.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 120: '(5) hybridization using labelled VNTR probe, and (6) detection of hybridized DNA fragments by autoradiography.'

questions.question: What is the key structural difference between ribonucleotides and deoxyribonucleotides that contributes to the greater chemical stability of DNA?
options: Deoxyribose lacks a 2'-OH group, making DNA less prone to catalytic cleavage and hydrolysis.
Ribose contains an extra phosphate group at the 3' position instead of a hydroxyl group.
Deoxyribose forms stronger hydrogen bonds between cytosine and guanine bases.
Ribonucleotides possess uracil which spontaneously degrades faster than thymine.
questions.explanation: The 2'-OH group present at every nucleotide in RNA is a reactive group that makes RNA labile and easily degradable. DNA, lacking the 2'-OH group at every sugar moiety (hence 'deoxy'), is chemically less reactive and structurally more stable.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 106: 'A 2'-OH group present at every nucleotide in RNA is a reactive group and makes RNA labile and easily degradable. DNA is chemically less reactive and structurally more stable when compared to RNA.'

questions.question: In Meselson and Stahl's experiment with 15N-labelled E. coli, after two generations in 14N medium, what was the proportion of radioactivity distributed in the extracted DNA bands?
options: 25% heavy DNA, 50% hybrid DNA, and 25% light DNA.
questions.explanation: After one generation (20 mins), 100% hybrid DNA was found. After two generations (40 mins), replication produced 4 DNA molecules: 2 hybrid (15N-14N) and 2 light (14N-14N), which translates to 50% hybrid and 50% light DNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 105: 'The E. coli divided... after 40 minutes... got two types of DNA molecules: light (14N-14N) and hybrid (15N-14N) (equal proportions).'

questions.question: Why did Hershey and Chase use radioactive 35S and 32P in their experiments with bacteriophage and E. coli?
options: 35S labels proteins (due to sulfur-containing amino acids) and 32P labels DNA (due to the phosphate backbone).
35S labels DNA and 32P labels the viral protein coat.
Both isotopes were used to label the protein coat exclusively while leaving the genetic material unlabelled.
32P was used because sulfur cannot be detected via radioactive tracing in biological molecules.
questions.explanation: Proteins contain sulfur (methionine, cysteine) but no phosphorus, so 35S labels protein. DNA contains phosphorus (in its phosphate backbone) but no sulfur, so 32P labels DNA. This differential labeling allowed them to prove DNA is the genetic material.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 104: 'They grew some viruses on a medium that contained radioactive phosphorus (32P) and some others on medium that contained radioactive sulfur (35S)... Viruses grown in the presence of radioactive phosphorus contained radioactive DNA but not protein because DNA contains phosphorus but protein does not.'

questions.question: Which of the following chemical components is NOT a part of a deoxynucleotide?
questions.explanation: A deoxynucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base, a deoxyribose sugar, and a phosphate group. Ribose sugar is found in ribonucleotides (RNA), not deoxyribonucleotides (DNA).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 96: A nucleotide has three components - a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar (ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA), and a phosphate group.

questions.question: In double-stranded DNA, the two chains have anti-parallel polarity. This means that:
options: Both chains run in the 5' to 3' direction
One chain runs in the 5' to 3' direction and the other in 3' to 5' direction
Both chains run in the 3' to 5' direction
The two chains are parallel but twisted in opposite directions
questions.explanation: The two strands of DNA have anti-parallel polarity, meaning if one chain has the polarity 5' -> 3', the other has 3' -> 5'.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 98: The two chains have anti-parallel polarity. It means, if one chain has the polarity 5'->3', the other has 3'->5'.

questions.question: The pitch of the DNA double helix (the length of one complete turn of the helix) is approximately:
questions.explanation: The pitch of the DNA helix is 3.4 nm (34 Angstroms), and it contains approximately 10 base pairs in each turn.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 98: The pitch of this helix is 3.4 nm and there are roughly 10 base pairs in each turn.

questions.question: During DNA replication in eukaryotes, replication fork moves along the template strand. The synthesis of DNA on the lagging strand occurs in short segments known as:
questions.explanation: On the template strand with 5'->3' polarity, DNA replication is discontinuous, producing short stretches of DNA called Okazaki fragments.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 106: These intermittently synthesized DNA segments, known as Okazaki fragments, are later joined by the enzyme DNA ligase.

questions.question: In the process of transcription in bacteria, which RNA polymerase is responsible for catalyzing the elongation of all types of RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA)?
questions.explanation: In bacteria, there is only a single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that catalyses transcription of all types of RNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 109: In bacteria, there is only a single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that catalyses transcription of all types of RNA.

questions.question: The presence of an untranslated region (UTR) in an mRNA is important for:
questions.explanation: UTRs are regions on mRNA that are not translated into protein but are required for efficient translation processes (present at both 5'-end and 3'-end).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 112: The mRNA also have some additional sequences that are not translated and are referred as untranslated regions (UTR). The UTRs are present at both 5'-end (before start codon) and at 3'-end (after stop codon). They are required for efficient translation process.

questions.question: In the lac operon, the repressor protein is synthesized all the time (constitutively) by which of the following genes?
questions.explanation: The 'i' gene in the lac operon codes for the repressor of the lac operon, and it is synthesized constitutively.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 116: The i gene codes for the repressor of the lac operon. The term 'i' does not refer to inducer rather it stands for inhibitor. 'i' gene is expressed constitutively, i.e., it is all the time being synthesized by the cell.

questions.question: What is the total estimated number of genes in human DNA according to the Human Genome Project findings?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project revealed that human genome contains 3000 million chemical base pairs, and estimated total genes to be 20,000 to 25,000.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5, Page 119: The total number of genes is estimated at 30,000 much lower than previous estimates of 80,000 to 140,000 genes. However, later it was revised to 20,000 to 25,000 genes.

questions.question: Which of the following chemical groups is present at the 5' end of a polynucleotide chain?
questions.explanation: At the 5' end of a polynucleotide chain, a free phosphate moiety is attached to the 5' carbon of the pentose sugar, whereas the 3' end bears a free -OH group.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 97: 'At one end of the chain (referred to as 5'-end of the polynucleotide chain) there has a free phosphate moiety at 5'-carbon position of ribose, while at the other end of the chain the sugar has a free OH of 3'-carbon position...'

questions.question: In Griffith's transformation experiment, which of the following strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae caused pneumonia and death when injected into mice, but did not do so when heat-killed?
options: Living R-strain combined with heat-killed S-strain
questions.explanation: The S-strain (smooth, mucous coat) is virulent and causes pneumonia and death. When heat-killed, it cannot cause disease, but living R-strain combined with heat-killed S-strain does cause death due to transformation.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 100: 'Mice infected with the S-strain (smooth, virulent) die from pneumonia caused... When injected heat-killed S-strain bacteria, mice did not die.'

questions.question: During DNA replication in Escherichia coli, the unwinding of the DNA duplex requires an enzyme. Which enzyme is primarily responsible for opening the helix?
questions.explanation: DNA replication requires a set of catalysts (enzymes). The unwinding of DNA is carried out by helicase, which breaks the hydrogen bonds between the strands.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 106: 'For long DNA molecules, since the two strands of DNA cannot be separated in its entire length (due to very high energy requirement), the replication occur within a small opening of the DNA helix, referred to as replication fork. DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalyse polymerisation only in one direction...'

questions.question: In the lac operon of Escherichia coli, the i gene codes for which of the following?
questions.explanation: In lac operon, the i gene codes for the repressor of the lac operon. The z gene codes for beta-galactosidase, y gene for permease, and a gene for transacetylase.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 117: 'The lac operon consists of one regulatory gene (the i gene - here the term i does not refer to inducer, rather it is related to inhibitor) and three structural genes (z, y, and a)... the i gene codes for the repressor of the lac operon.'

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the genetic code?
options: Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, hence the code is degenerate.
The codon is ambiguous, meaning one codon can code for more than one amino acid.
UAG acts as the initiator codon for protein synthesis.
The genetic code is overlapping in prokaryotes and non-overlapping in eukaryotes.
questions.explanation: The genetic code is degenerate because some amino acids are coded by multiple codons. It is unambiguous (one codon specifies only one amino acid), non-overlapping, and AUG is the initiator codon.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 111: 'some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, hence the code is degenerate.'

questions.question: What is the primary function of hnRNA processing in eukaryotic transcription?
options: Removal of introns (splicing) and addition of cap and tail
Addition of codons at the 3' end to lengthen the reading frame
questions.explanation: In eukaryotes, primary transcripts (hnRNA) contain both exons and introns. Introns are removed by splicing, and capping and tailing are performed to form functional mRNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 110: 'In eukaryotes... the primary transcripts contain both exon and intron and are non-functional. Hence, it is subjected to a process called splicing where the introns are removed and exons are joined in a defined order.'

questions.question: Which radioactive isotopes were used by Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase to conclusively prove that DNA is the genetic material?
questions.explanation: Hershey and Chase used radioactive phosphorus (32P) to label DNA and radioactive sulfur (35S) to label proteins in bacteriophages to distinguish between DNA and protein.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 101-102: 'They grew some viruses on a medium that contained radioactive phosphorus (32P) and some others on medium containing radioactive sulfur (35S)...'

questions.question: In a double stranded DNA, if the percentage of cytosine is 18%, what will be the percentage of adenine according to Chargaff's rules?
questions.explanation: According to Chargaff's rules, [A] = [T] and [G] = [C]. Since C = 18%, G must be 18%. Total G + C = 36%. Therefore, A + T = 100 - 36 = 64%. Since A = T, Adenine = 64 / 2 = 32%.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 97-98: 'Chargaff's rules for double stranded DNA state that the ratio between Adenine and Thymine and guanine and cytosine are constant and equals one (A=T and G=C).'

questions.question: Which enzyme is responsible for joining the Okazaki fragments during DNA replication?
questions.explanation: DNA ligase is the enzyme that seals the nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone by joining the discontinuously synthesized Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 107: 'The discontinuously synthesised fragments are later joined by the enzyme DNA ligase.'

questions.question: In RNA, which nitrogenous base replaces Thymine found in DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA contains ribose sugar and uracil in place of thymine (5-methyluracil) which is characteristically present in DNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 96: 'DNA stores genetic information whereas RNA mostly functions as a messenger. Uracil is present in RNA at the place of Thymine.'

questions.question: Which of the following chemical components distinguishes a ribonucleotide from a deoxyribonucleotide in terms of sugar structure?
options: Presence of a 2'-OH group in the ribose sugar
Presence of a 3'-OH group in the deoxyribose sugar
Presence of a 5'-phosphate group in the ribose sugar
Presence of a 1'-nitrogenous base linkage in the deoxyribose sugar
questions.explanation: A ribonucleotide has a ribose sugar with a hydroxyl (-OH) group at the 2' position, whereas a deoxyribose sugar lacks this oxygen atom, having only a hydrogen atom at the 2' position.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.1, page 96: 'A deoxyribose sugar has an additional OH group at 2'-posn in the ribose... wait, RNA has 2'-OH in ribose.'

questions.question: During DNA replication, RNA primers are necessary because:
options: DNA polymerase can catalyze addition only in the 3' to 5' direction
DNA polymerase cannot initiate replication on its own without a free 3'-OH group
RNA primers provide the template strand for leading strand synthesis
RNA primers permanently become part of the completed DNA molecule
questions.explanation: DNA polymerases are unable to initiate the synthesis of a DNA strand de novo; they require an existing free 3'-OH group provided by an RNA primer to begin adding nucleotides.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.2, page 105: DNA polymerases on their own cannot initiate the process of replication.

questions.question: In the lac operon, if a mutation occurs in the regulator gene (i) that produces a repressor protein unable to bind to the operator region, what will be the phenotype of the operon in the absence of an inducer?
questions.explanation: A mutant repressor that cannot bind to the operator fails to block RNA polymerase, leading to constitutive (continuous) expression of the structural genes even when lactose (inducer) is absent.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.8, page 117: Regulation of lac operon by repressor and inducer.

questions.question: What is the primary role of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases during translation?
options: Binding the mRNA codon to the ribosome A-site
Charging the tRNA with its specific amino acid
Forming the peptide bond between adjacent amino acids
Translating the stop codons into release factors
questions.explanation: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are enzymes responsible for charging tRNA molecules by covalently linking them to their cognate (specific) amino acids, which is essential for the first phase of translation.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.5, page 113: 'For chargng of tRNA (aminoacylation)... amino acid is activated in the presence of ATP and linked to its cognate tRNA...'

questions.question: Which of the following properties of genetic code ensures that a change in a single nucleotide does not necessarily change the entire downstream reading frame, unless it is an insertion or deletion?
options: The code is comma-less and non-overlapping
questions.explanation: Because the genetic code is read in a contiguous, non-overlapping manner (comma-less), a point mutation (substitution) alters only a single codon, whereas insertions and deletions cause a reading frame shift.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.5, page 111: Salient features of genetic code - triplet, unambiguous, degenerate, non-overlapping.

questions.question: In Griffith's transforming principle experiment, why did mice infected with a mixture of heat-killed Smooth (S) strain and live Rough (R) strain die from pneumonia?
options: The heat-killed S strain was revived by the living mouse tissue
Live R strain bacteria were transformed into virulent S strain by taking up genetic material from the heat-killed S strain
Heat-killed S strain bacteria mutated spontaneously back to the virulent form
The live R strain secreted a toxin that killed the mouse synergistically with heat-killed S proteins
questions.explanation: Genetic material (DNA) from the heat-killed virulent S strain was taken up by the living non-virulent R strain, transforming them into virulent smooth-coated bacteria that killed the mice.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.1, page 100: Griffith's experiment showing bacterial transformation.

questions.question: During transcription in eukaryotes, which RNA polymerase is specifically responsible for transcribing 5S rRNA, tRNA, and snRNAs?
questions.explanation: In eukaryotes, RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA, and small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs). RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S), and RNA polymerase II transcribes precursors of mRNA (hnRNA).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.6, page 114: Table/Text describing eukaryotic RNA polymerases.

questions.question: What is the exact function of 'capping' during post-transcriptional modification of eukaryotic hnRNA?
options: Addition of an adenylate residue at the 3' end in a template-independent manner
Addition of methylguanosine triphosphate at the 5' end
Removal of non-coding introns through spliceosomes
Formation of hairpin loops for transcription termination
questions.explanation: Capping involves adding an unusual nucleotide (methylguanosine triphosphate) to the 5' end of hnRNA during post-transcriptional processing.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.6, page 114: 'In capping an unusual nucleotide (methyl guanosine triphosphate) is added to the 5'-end of hnRNA.'

questions.question: Meselson and Stahl used heavy isotope 15N to prove semi-conservative DNA replication in E. coli. After how many generations of growth in 14N medium did they observe equal amounts of hybrid (15N-14N) and light (14N-14N) DNA molecules?
questions.explanation: After 1 generation, all DNA was hybrid (15N/14N). After 2 generations (40 minutes), half the DNA was hybrid and half was light (14N/14N).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.2, page 103: Meselson and Stahl experiment results after 20 and 40 minutes.

questions.question: In a polynucleotide chain, a phosphate moiety is linked to the carbon atom of the sugar of the same nucleotide at which position?
questions.explanation: The backbone of a DNA/RNA strand is formed by sugar-phosphate chains where the phosphate group is linked to the 3'-carbon of one sugar and the 5'-carbon of the next sugar via phosphodiester bonds.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, Section 6.1, page 96: 'The backbone in a polynucleotide chain is due to sugar and phosphates... linked by 3'-5' phosphodiester linkage.'

questions.question: If the base sequence of one strand of DNA is 5'-ATGCGTAC-3', then what will be the sequence and polarity of the complementary strand synthesized during replication?
questions.explanation: Due to base pairing rules (A pairs with T through two hydrogen bonds, and G pairs with C through three hydrogen bonds) and antiparallel polarity of the two DNA strands, the complementary strand for 5'-ATGCGTAC-3' will have 3'-TACGCATG-5' sequence.
questions.ncertEvidence: The two strands have anti-parallel polarity... Adenine forms two hydrogen bonds with Thymine from opposite strand and Guanine is bonded with Cytosine with three H-bonds.

questions.question: In a Hershey and Chase experiment, radioactive 32P was used to label bacteriophage DNA. After centrifugation, where was the radioactivity primarily detected and why?
options: In the bacterial pellet, because DNA entered the bacterial cells.
In the supernatant, because viral coats remained outside the cells.
In the supernatant, because DNA dissolved in the medium.
In the bacterial pellet, because viral protein coats entered the cells.
questions.explanation: Bacteria that were infected with viruses that had radioactive DNA were radioactive, indicating that DNA was the material that passed from the virus to the bacteria. Thus, radioactivity was found in the bacterial pellet.
questions.ncertEvidence: Bacteria that were infected with viruses that had radioactive DNA were radioactive, indicating that DNA was the material that passed from the virus to the bacteria. Hence, the pellet gave radioactive signal.

questions.question: During DNA replication, RNA primer is required because:
options: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing free 3'-OH group.
RNA polymerase synthesizes the entire leading strand.
DNA polymerase lacks proofreading activity without RNA.
RNA primers provide energy for phosphodiester bond formation.
questions.explanation: DNA polymerases are unable to initiate replication on their own; they strictly require a free 3'-OH group of an existing nucleotide primer (usually RNA) to extend the chain.
questions.ncertEvidence: DNA polymerases on their own cannot initiate the process of replication. Also the replication does not initiate randomly at any place in DNA.

questions.question: If Meselson and Stahl's experiment is carried out with 15N E. coli transferred to 14N medium for 40 minutes (generation time = 20 minutes), what proportion of DNA molecules will be completely light (14N-14N)?
questions.explanation: After 1 generation (20 mins), hybrid DNA is formed. After 2 generations (40 mins), out of 4 total DNA molecules, 2 are hybrid (15N-14N) and 2 are completely light (14N-14N). Therefore, 2/4 = 50% are completely light.
questions.ncertEvidence: Meselson and Stahl's experiment showing semi-conservative DNA replication where 14N-14N and 15N-14N DNA are separated by CsCl density gradient centrifugation.

questions.question: A segment of DNA has 100 base pairs and contains 20 adenine bases. How many phosphodiester linkages are present in this entire double-stranded DNA molecule?
questions.explanation: A double-stranded DNA with 100 base pairs has 200 nucleotides per strand, but total nucleotides = 200. In each strand of length n, there are (n-1) phosphodiester bonds. For two strands of 100 nucleotides each, total phosphodiester bonds = (100-1) + (100-1) = 99 + 99 = 198.
questions.ncertEvidence: Backbone of polynucleotide chain is due to sugar-phosphate... phosphodiester bond links nucleotides.

questions.question: In the lac operon, if a mutation occurs in the promoter gene such that RNA polymerase cannot bind to it, what will be the phenotypic consequence?
options: The structural genes (z, y, a) will not be transcribed even in the presence of lactose.
The structural genes will be constitutively expressed.
The repressor protein will not be synthesized.
Lactose will not be able to enter the cell.
questions.explanation: The promoter is the binding site for RNA polymerase. If the promoter is mutated and cannot bind RNA polymerase, transcription of the downstream structural genes cannot be initiated under any condition.
questions.ncertEvidence: Promoter is the binding site for RNA polymerase for transcription... in absence of promoter, transcription does not occur.

questions.question: What would happen if histones were mutated to carry a net neutral charge instead of a positive charge?
options: Binding of DNA to histones would be severely impaired, disrupting nucleosome formation.
Transcription would be permanently switched off.
DNA replication would become entirely conservative.
RNA would bind to histones instead of DNA.
questions.explanation: Histones are rich in basic amino acids lysine and arginine, imparting a positive charge. DNA is negatively charged. A neutral charge would reduce the electrostatic attraction, preventing stable nucleosome core formation.
questions.ncertEvidence: Histones are positively charged basic proteins... DNA is negatively charged and wrapped around positively charged histone octamer to form nucleosome.

questions.question: During transcription in a eukaryote, hnRNA undergoes capping. What is added at the 5'-end of hnRNA during capping?
questions.explanation: In capping, an unusual nucleotide (methyl guanosine triphosphate) is added to the 5'-end of hnRNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: In capping an unusual nucleotide (methyl guanosine triphosphate) is added to the 5'-end of hnRNA.

questions.question: If the genetic code is degenerate, what does it signify regarding codons and amino acids?
options: An amino acid can be coded by more than one codon.
A single codon can code for more than one amino acid.
The code is universal across all living organisms.
Codons have no punctuation between them.
questions.explanation: Degeneracy of the genetic code means that some amino acids are coded by more than one codon (e.g., serine is coded by six codons).
questions.ncertEvidence: Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, hence the code is degenerate.

questions.question: Which of the following RNA molecules acts as both an adapter molecule and has structural/catalytic roles during translation?
options: tRNA acts as an adapter, while rRNA plays structural and catalytic roles (like 23S rRNA as ribozyme).
mRNA acts as an adapter and rRNA acts as structural RNA.
snRNA acts as an adapter and tRNA acts as catalytic RNA.
tRNA acts as structural and mRNA acts as adapter.
questions.explanation: tRNA is known as the adapter molecule that reads the code and brings amino acids. rRNA provides structural support and in some cases catalytic activity (e.g., 23S rRNA is a ribozyme for peptide bond formation).
questions.ncertEvidence: tRNA-the adapter molecule... ribosomal RNA (rRNA) play structural and catalytic role (23S rRNA in bacteria is a ribozyme).

questions.question: Which of the following nitrogenous bases is present in RNA but absent in DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA contains uracil in place of thymine, which is found in DNA.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 109: 'DNA and RNA ... Adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine (for DNA) and uracil (for RNA).'

questions.question: The length of DNA double helix in a typical mammalian cell is approximately:
questions.explanation: The total length of DNA in a mammalian cell is calculated by multiplying the total number of base pairs (6.6 x 10^9 bp) by the distance between two consecutive base pairs (0.34 x 10^-9 m), which equals approximately 2.2 meters.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 103: 'If you length of DNA double helix in a typical mammalian cell is calculated (simply by multiplying the total number of bp with distance between two consecutive bp, i.e., 6.6 x 10^9 bp x 0.34 x 10^-9 m/bp), it comes out to be approximately 2.2 meters.'

questions.question: In the process of transcription in E. coli, which enzyme is solely responsible for catalyzing the elongation of all types of RNA?
questions.explanation: Unlike eukaryotes which have multiple RNA polymerases, bacteria (E. coli) have only one DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that catalyses transcription of all types of RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA).
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 114: 'In bacteria, there is only one DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that catalyses transcription of all types of RNA.'

questions.question: The specific amino acid attached to the 3'-end of a tRNA molecule is determined by:
questions.explanation: tRNA has an amino acid acceptor end (3'-end) to which it binds its specific amino acid.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 116: '...tRNA has an anticodon loop that has bases complementary to the code, and an amino acid acceptor end to which it binds to its amino acid.'

questions.question: In the lac operon, the i gene codes for which of the following?
questions.explanation: The 'i' gene in the lac operon codes for the repressor of the lac operon.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 117: 'The lac operon consists of one regulatory gene (the i gene - here the term i does not refer to inducer, rather it is derived from the word inhibitor) and three structural genes (z, y, and a). The i gene codes for the repressor of the lac operon.'

questions.question: Frederick Griffith proved the phenomenon of bacterial transformation using which organism?
questions.explanation: Frederick Griffith (1928) used Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) to demonstrate bacterial transformation in mice.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 101: 'In 1928, Frederick Griffith, in a series of experiments with Streptococcus pneumoniae (bacterium responsible for pneumonia), witnessed a miraculous transformation in the bacteria.'

questions.question: Satellite DNA is classified into categories such as micro-satellites and mini-satellites based on:
options: Length of the segment, number of repetitive units, and genomic composition
questions.explanation: Satellite DNA is classified into many categories such as micro-satellites, mini-satellites, etc., based on base composition, length of repetitive segment, and number of repetitive units.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 120: 'Depending on base composition (A:T rich or G:C rich), length of segment, and number of repetitive units, the bulk DNA has peaks during density gradient centrifugation. These sequence DNA are classified into categories, such as micro-satellites, mini-satellites etc.'

questions.question: Which of the following scientists conclusively proved that DNA is the genetic material using radioactive isotopes of phosphorus and sulfur?
questions.explanation: Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952) worked with bacteriophages and used radioactive phosphorus (32P) and sulfur (35S) to prove that DNA is the genetic material.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 103: 'The unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material came from the experiments of Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952). They worked with viruses that infect bacteria called bacteriophages.'

questions.question: During DNA replication, unwinding of the DNA double helix is facilitated by which enzyme?
questions.explanation: The unwinding of the DNA strand to form the replication fork is carried out by DNA helicase.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, Page 108: 'For long DNA molecules, since the two strands of DNA cannot be separated in its entire length (due to high energy requirement), the replication occur within a small opening of the DNA helix, referred to as replication fork. The DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalyses polymerisation only in one direction...'

questions.question: Which of the following conditions of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium operates so that frequency of an allele in a population remains constant from generation to generation?
options: Absence of mutation, migration, and selection
High rate of gene migration between populations
Frequent genetic drift due to small population size
questions.explanation: According to the Hardy-Weinberg principle, allele frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation in the absence of gene flow or gene migration, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, and natural selection.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, page 136: 'The Hardy-Weinberg principle... states that allele frequencies in a population are stable and is constant from generation to generation. The gene pool... remains a constant. This is called genetic equilibrium. Disturbance in genetic equilibrium, or change in frequency of alleles in a population would then be interpreted as resulting in evolution.'

questions.question: Which of the following scientists gave the theory of chemical evolution of life, proposing that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules?
questions.explanation: Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (e.g., RNA, protein, etc.) and that formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, page 126: 'Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (e.g., RNA, protein, etc.) and that formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution...'

questions.question: What was the specific mixture of gases used by S.L. Miller in his 1953 electric discharge experiment to simulate primitive Earth conditions?
options: CH4, NH3, H2, and water vapor
CO2, O2, N2, and water vapor
CH4, O2, NH3, and hydrogen sulfide
questions.explanation: In 1953, S.L. Miller created electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapor at 800°C and observed the formation of amino acids.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, page 126: 'In 1953, S.L. Miller, an American scientist created electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800°C.'

questions.question: Homologous organs, such as the forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetahs, and humans, share a similar anatomical structure because they:
options: Perform identical functions in different environments
Share a common ancestry with similar developmental origin
Resulted from independent mutations in similar habitats
questions.explanation: Homologous organs have the same structural plan and origin (indicating common ancestry) though they may perform different functions due to adaptation to different needs. This represents divergent evolution.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, page 128: 'The whales, bats, Cheetah and human (all mammals) share similarities in the pattern of bones of forelimbs. These forelimbs perform different functions in these animals... Such organs are homologous organs... homologous indicates common ancestry.'

questions.question: Which of the following pairs represents analogous organs resulting from convergent evolution?
options: Thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita
Forelimbs of whales and forelimbs of humans
Wings of butterflies and wings of birds
Hearts of bats and hearts of rabbits
questions.explanation: Wings of an insect (butterfly) and wings of a bird are analogous organs; they are not anatomically similar structures though they perform similar functions (flying), representing convergent evolution.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, page 129: 'Analogy... is not anatomically similar though they perform similar functions. Examples... wings of butterfly and of birds...'

questions.question: Industrial melanism in the peppered moth (Biston betularia) in England serves as an excellent field observation for demonstrating:
questions.explanation: Before industrialization, white-winged moths were more abundant than dark-winged forms; after industrialization, dark-winged forms became more abundant due to camouflage against soot-covered trees, proving natural selection.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, page 130: 'Before industrialisation... thick growth of white-coloured lichen covered the trees... dark-coloured moth could be easily picked out by predators... After industrialisation... tree trunks became dark due to industrial smoke... This showed that in a mixed population, those that can better adapt, survive and increase in population size. Remember that no variant is completely wiped out.'

questions.question: What term is used to describe the evolutionary process where distinct species originating from a common ancestor rapidly adapt to diverse geographical habitats?
questions.explanation: Adaptive radiation is an evolutionary process in which an ancestral stock radiates into different species radiating to other geographical areas, such as Darwin's finches or Australian marsupials.
questions.ncertEvidence: NCERT Class XII, Chapter 6, page 131: 'This process of evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from a point and literally radiating to other areas of geography (habitats) is called adaptive radiation.'

questions.question: According to Hugo de Vries, what causes evolution to occur through sudden, single-step large mutations, unlike Darwin's concept of slow, gradual variations?
options: Natural selection of minor continuous variations
questions.explanation: Hugo de Vries believed mutations caused evolution and not the minor variations that Darwin talked about. Mutations are random and directionless, whereas de Vries called single-step large mutations 'saltation'.
